operator_plays.mechanism: Ingest fragmented county dockets, probate registries, unclaimed property ledgers, and public APIs to surface uncontested claims or high-intent B2B triggers before manual competitors.

State controller ledgers
Public licensing & entity APIs

operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
inputs: Tax-sale excess proceeds ledgers
Unclaimed property & judgment dockets
Surplus auction manifests
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts

Claim approval rate
Days from filing to disbursement

platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules

operator_plays.name: B2B Class-Action & Antitrust Settlement Contingency Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Monitor multibillion-dollar corporate antitrust and commercial class-action settlement funds (payment-card interchange, freight, auto parts, commercial insurance, SaaS) where 85–90% of eligible small businesses never file, and recover verified payouts on a 25–33% contingency fee.

Contingency claim-preparation & court-authorized third-party filing agreements

Claim acceptance rate by court-appointed administrator (%)
Net contingency fee per operator hour invested

platform_risks.failure_mode: Claim rejection, administrator audit hold, or court cap on third-party filer fees

platform_risks.impact: Delayed payout disbursement or court-mandated fee reduction

platform_risks.fallback: File strictly for verified operating businesses with primary processor/vendor statements and use court-approved third-party claim-filing riders

operator_plays.mechanism: Scraping federal DOE/EPA interconnection queues, state film offices, and historic-preservation registries to originate transferable tax credits (IRC § 6418 Clean Energy Investment/Production Credits, Georgia/Louisiana Film Credits, State Historic Rehab & Brownfield Credits) from cash-strapped project developers at $0.82–$0.88 on the dollar and flipping them in simultaneous escrow closings to corporate and HNW taxpayers at $0.92–$0.96 on the dollar.

Execute a simultaneous bilateral escrow closing with a corporate taxpayer at $0.92–$0.95 on the dollar—saving the buyer 5–8% guaranteed on their tax bill while capturing a 400–800 bps riskless spread ($40k–$80k per $1M block)

Net retained principal/brokerage spread (400–800 bps) per closed tranche
Days in escrow from developer IRS registration number issuance to wire settlement

chapters.question_prompt: What qualifies as unclaimed property, how does it reach state custody, and where should an operator begin searching?
chapters.title: Unclaimed Property Fundamentals and Search Entry Points
chapters.subtitle: Dormant assets, escheatment, uncashed checks, warrants, recovery terminology, fund categories, and official search databases
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the asset class is custodial money: holders unable to deliver wages, deposits, or securities must send a due diligence notice and remit to the state after a dormancy clock of one year for payroll and three to five for bank accounts, and states hold it with no expiration. About $70 billion sits in state custody and one in seven Americans has a stake, yet the median claim is about $100 against a $2,080 average. Street mechanics start at MissingMoney.com, then unclaimed.org for states like California and Pennsylvania, then federal registries for wages, pensions, FHA refunds, failed banks, and bankruptcy courts. Disagreements center on fees, where consumer voices call self-filing free and paid help unnecessary while finders operate under caps of 10 to 30 percent, and on Treasury Hunt, which some still recommend and others call retired.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator working this lane starts from the same base fact: holders cannot keep money they owe and cannot deliver. Hoang Le frames unclaimed property as any asset a company, bank, or government agency owed, tried to deliver, and could not, usually because the owner moved, changed a name, or lost touch, after which the holder must transfer it to the state in a process called escheatment [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:01:06]. Base_Rate sharpens the point with an uncashed check: the paper goes stale after 180 days under UCC section 4-404, but the underlying obligation does not expire with it, so the payer carries it as a liability until the dormancy clock forces a report and remittance [RycXVSWGZ3I @ 00:00:48]. The Lorman panel adds the holder-side doctrine that matters when you argue about what is actually claimable: modern laws are custodial, not true escheat, so title never moves from owner to state, and the state pays owners who later come forward and prove a valid claim [2TghvbJiOis @ 00:14:20]. Money Grammar lands in the same place for the consumer side, calling the state a custodial holder that keeps property in perpetuity until the owner or a legal heir steps forward [5l8zepw8oWY @ 00:04:03]. That custodial frame is why operators treat old files as live inventory rather than dead leads.

The dormancy clock is the second point of agreement, and the numbers line up across camps. Hoang Le puts wages, payroll checks, and utility deposits at roughly one year, matured life insurance at three years, bank accounts and securities at three to five, and travelers checks at up to fifteen in some states [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:01:58]. The Lorman panel confirms the one-year payroll rule in almost every state, counted from the date of issuance, and reports the trend is toward shorter clocks: states that once sat near fifteen years are moving from five to three, with Maine running two-year periods on gift cards [2TghvbJiOis @ 00:21:48]. Before the clock runs out, the holder owes a due diligence notice; Hoang Le times that letter at 60 to 180 days before the reporting deadline, mailed to the last known address, which is exactly why movers never see it [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:02:28]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 translates the same mechanics into recovery-agent terms: holders like Chase Bank or Safeco Life Insurance run a due diligence window Wilkerson pegs at 6 to 24 months, then the property escheats, and only after the 12 to 24 month dormancy period can the investigator step in to assist a claimant [-VDHxOAAA7A @ 00:04:56].

On the hunt itself, nearly every speaker gives the same entry order: state databases first, every state touched, then federal registries. Money Grammar warns there is no single place to look, so you search every state where you lived, worked, or established a business, because the system is decentralized and the state will not come looking for you [5l8zepw8oWY @ 00:05:42]. This Guy Knows Tech warns that state portals hold no federal assets, which is why millions of people search one state registry, find zero results, and wrongly assume nothing is coming [74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:02:47]. On fees, the consumer-side voices agree that filing with the state costs nothing, while the recovery-side voices confirm the paid lane is real: Hoang Le says licensed locators, sometimes called heir finders, are regulated in most states and typically capped around 10 percent, and a legitimate one never collects before the owner is paid [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:07:03]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut, working the business since 2018, argues the agent role is crucial precisely because states do a poor job of notifying owners, with some funds sitting since the 60s after a mailed letter most owners ignore or never receive [7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:02:11]. That gap between free self-service and owner inertia is where the agent fee lives.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: MissingMoney.com is the first keystroke in almost every playbook. Hoang Le calls it the free national database run by the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators and the single fastest first step, since one query hits most participating states at once [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:03:16]. Money Missed flags the hole in that net: a few states, including California and Pennsylvania, run their own separate systems, so the second stop is unclaimed.org, where an interactive map links straight into every state's official program [sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:08:19]. Diane Lee of WSPA 7News gives the field-level workaround on the multi-state site: enter the name, choose the state from the dropdown, and if that state is not listed in bold, select it anyway to get a direct link to the state's own unclaimed property site [VF97sp7MzAw @ 00:03:06]. The money then hides in name variants. This Guy Knows Tech reports state treasuries sitting on millions under misspelled names, inverted first and last names, and outdated nicknames, where an old utility company logging Jonathan as John can strand a $500 deposit indefinitely [74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:02:15]. Money Missed's own drill adds maiden names, nicknames, middle initials, and junior or senior suffixes on every pass, so treat a single clean-name search as incomplete.

State portals stop at state money, so the second sweep is federal. Money Missed lists the separate federal slices: unpaid final paychecks through the Department of Labor, forgotten pensions through the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, unclaimed VA life insurance, FHA mortgage insurance refunds through HUD, failed bank and credit union deposits through the FDIC or NCUA, and tax refunds that generally must be claimed within three years of the original filing deadline [sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:09:19]. On savings bonds, Dollar Decoded reports the Treasury holding around $29 billion in bonds that stopped earning interest, says the old Treasury Hunt site was retired in 2025, and routes searchers to the state unclaimed property office instead [QVgTN5Lip0o @ 00:05:34]. For lost 401(k) money when the old employer is unreachable, Josie Sturman of InvestigateTV points to the Form 5500 a company files with the federal government about its plan; the Department of Labor lookup puts the plan administrator and a phone number on the first page [YWsshlY3kF4 @ 00:01:36]. This Guy Knows Tech pushes into bankruptcy court registries, where returned distribution checks owed to creditors, vendors, contractors, and even tenants sit in federal court accounts across individual districts until someone claims them [74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:08:43].

Once a match hits, the paperwork scales with the size and type of the claim. Hoang Le says smaller claims often clear online with minimal documentation, while larger claims, securities, safe deposit boxes, and claims filed for someone else usually require notarized documentation proving identity and legal right to the asset [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:05:10]. Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed lists the standard packet as a photo ID, the Social Security number, and proof of residence at the listed address, where an old bill or lease works, plus a death certificate and heirship proof for a relative's property [J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:04:47]. On the agent side, Eric Richardson says some states require you to register as a finder, which means fingerprints and a background check, and puts state-level payouts at 16 to 120 days; the county-level lane needs no registration, often runs off a one-page form, and carries lower values but low competition [7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:02:36]. David Wilkerson keeps the economics in perspective: knowing the vocabulary will not make or break the business, because the money is made in contacting claimants, following up, and converting, and confidence with the terms helps an agent project certainty of outcome on the call [-VDHxOAAA7A @ 00:01:12].

callout.title: Where the Hidden Matches and Hidden Value Live
callout.body: Operator-level edges pulled from recoveries, heir cases, and agent-side workflow reported by the practitioners.
items: Search the dead, not just the living: Illinois' record $11 million Joseph Stancak estate required investigators to go back five generations to find 119 relatives across the US, Poland, and Slovakia [Money Missed — sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:03:30].

Expect disbelief on first contact even when the money is real: South Carolina's treasurer found an heir owed more than $763,000 who assumed the call was a scam and almost hung up [Money Missed — sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:03:49].

Escheated securities stop tracking the market: stocks are often sold after turnover and the owner usually receives the cash value at sale, not today's price, so speed matters [Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed — J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:03:15].

Make the state unclaimed property office your best friend, because it processes claims and handles disbursement payouts to claimants or locators and can make the work smooth or painful [Surplus Funds 101 — -VDHxOAAA7A @ 00:05:15].

sop_steps.title: Run the multi-state sweep first
sop_steps.action: Search MissingMoney.com under the current legal name, then follow any non-bold state to its own official site.
sop_steps.detail: Hoang Le calls MissingMoney.com the single fastest first step for most people [Hoang Le CFP, EA, Real Estate Agent — kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:03:16]; WSPA 7News shows the state dropdown and the direct link for states not listed in bold [WSPA 7News — VF97sp7MzAw @ 00:03:06].

sop_steps.title: Expand every state and every name variant
sop_steps.action: Re-run searches for each state lived, worked, or banked in, plus maiden names, nicknames, misspellings, business names, and deceased parents or grandparents.
sop_steps.detail: The variant and relative drill comes from [Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed — J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:04:10]; for common names, add the city and state lived in to filter out strangers sharing the name [Money Missed — sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:10:14].

sop_steps.title: Sweep federal and niche registries separately
sop_steps.action: Check Department of Labor wages, PBGC pensions, VA life insurance, HUD FHA refunds, FDIC or NCUA failed institutions, and bankruptcy court registries.
sop_steps.detail: Federal slices each hold their own records outside state databases [Money Missed — sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:09:19]; returned bankruptcy distribution checks get deposited into the court registry [This Guy Knows Tech — 74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:08:43].

sop_steps.title: File the ID packet and recheck yearly
sop_steps.action: Submit photo ID, Social Security number, and proof of the listed address, add heirship documents for relatives, then re-run all searches at least once a year.
sop_steps.detail: Proof of address can be an old bill or lease [Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed — J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:04:47]; Diana Cheban of the Virginia Department of Treasury recommends checking the system at least once a year [InvestigateTV — IhEPmIRt3Ak @ 00:03:02].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the unclaimed-funds world is whether an owner should ever pay a finder. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 frames recovery agents as people turning a hobby into a full-time business, assisting owners in reclaiming property for a fee or percentage of recovered funds, and notes that states label them heir finders, locators, or investigators [-VDHxOAAA7A @ 00:02:20]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut justifies the cut by arguing that states hold the money and do not do a good job notifying people, with funds probably sitting since the 60s behind a mailed letter most owners never see or never receive [7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:01:57]. Money Grammar takes the opposite line flatly: locators monitor public databases and contact individuals offering recovery for a percentage, and there is absolutely no need to pay because the exact same searches and claims cost zero when filed directly with the state [5l8zepw8oWY @ 00:07:36]. This Guy Knows Tech goes further, warning that anyone demanding upfront cash or a 20% locator fee is charging for work an owner can do in five minutes on an official registry [74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:09:15]. Net read: the finder's edge sits in the notification gap Richardson describes, not in any data the public cannot reach.

Practitioners also report different fee ceilings and conflicting pictures of how hard states hunt for owners. Hoang Le says licensed asset locators, sometimes called heir finders, are regulated in most states and typically capped around 10% of the property's value, and a legitimate one will never ask for payment before the owner receives the money [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:07:03]. Money Missed reports a wider registered-and-capped band, commonly 10 to 30%, describing paid finders as not illegal but never necessary [sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:12:17]. On outreach, Money Grammar insists the state will not actively search owners out and that the responsibility for starting recovery lies entirely with the individual [5l8zepw8oWY @ 00:05:42]. InvestigateTV reports the opposite on the ground: two Virginia residents who had never met each got unexpected calls from the state's Treasury Department, one caller had been searching for weeks, and both calls were legitimate and both paid off, one from a 1980s insurance policy and one from a late mother's estate [IhEPmIRt3Ak @ 00:00:34]. For a locator, that means the competition in some states is the treasury itself, which can reach a claimant first and charge nothing. Fee pitches also collide with Hoang Le's point that owners can verify a match themselves for free before agreeing to work with anyone.

Timing numbers diverge more than any other figure the speakers quote. Money Grammar anchors dormancy at often around five years before a holder must report and transfer the asset [5l8zepw8oWY @ 00:00:00], while Hoang Le breaks it out by asset: wages, payroll checks, and utility deposits after just one year, life insurance about three years after the policy matures, most checking, savings, and securities accounts three to five years, and travelers checks up to 15 years in some states [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:01:58]. Lorman's presenters report the direction of travel is shorter clocks, from around 15 years in many states originally down to five, then three, and even two-year periods for gift cards in Maine, because of the revenue-driven nature of these laws [2TghvbJiOis @ 00:21:29]. The tool list splits too. Hoang Le's checklist still routes matured savings bond hunters to the Treasury Hunt tool, but Dollar Decoded reports Treasury Hunt was retired in 2025 and that bond searches now start with the state unclaimed property office, pegging Treasury's stranded bonds at around $29 billion [QVgTN5Lip0o @ 00:05:34], a figure that already conflicts with Hoang Le's $32 billion estimate. Operators running older scripts are sending claimants to a dead tool and quoting mismatched market sizes.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common failure the speakers describe is the notice that never lands. Hoang Le explains that holders must mail a due diligence letter to the last known address, usually 60 to 180 days before the deadline, and if the owner moved without updating an old bank or employer, that letter never arrives and the account quietly transfers to the state [kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:02:28]. Money Making Juggernaut sees the same break in tax-sale surplus work: counties send excess-proceeds notices to the very property that was just foreclosed, where the former owners most likely no longer live [7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:04:00]. The second leak is data quality. This Guy Knows Tech reports that state treasuries hold millions of dollars under misspelled names, inverted first and last names, and outdated nicknames, so a single missed letter can leave a $500 deposit in state custody indefinitely [74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:02:15]. Dollar Decoded's walkthrough proves the point: an $800 security deposit was listed under Maya Rodriguez with a typo, and a plain search would have missed it entirely [QVgTN5Lip0o @ 00:03:41]. The practical failure is searching once, under one current legal name, in one current state, then concluding nothing exists. The speakers who address variations push maiden names, nicknames, misspellings, and every state lived, worked, or banked in.

Economics checks cut hard against the jackpot pitch. Money Missed cites NAUPA data putting the average claim at $2,080 but the median, the more typical claim, at only about $100, with a handful of large recoveries dragging the average up [sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:00:39]. An InvestigateTV anchor found $420 in their own name and openly went back and forth on whether the search was worth it before settling on yes [YWsshlY3kF4 @ 00:02:22]. Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed warns that stocks and other securities are often sold after they are turned over, so the owner usually gets the cash value from the sale date rather than today's price, which makes delay itself a loss [J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:03:15]. On the surplus side, Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut says second mortgages and liens can swallow a foreclosure surplus, so operators must do due diligence and verify a real surplus exists before chasing it, and should use an attorney on judicial and non-judicial mortgage foreclosure files [7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:04:58]. Cash flow is slow regardless: Richardson pegs claim payouts at 16 to 120 days. For an agent working on a percentage, a $100 median file with a four-month payout is the baseline unit, not the exception.

Holder-side traps are where small balances turn punitive. Unclaimed Money Recovery describes a live case where a state audit found one employee had failed to cash a $149 expense reimbursement check, and the state extrapolated it into a $2 million assessment, with due diligence penalties reaching up to 50% of the property turned over [ZDSZHh3DZGs @ 00:02:13]. The same firm puts audit look-back periods at 10 to 20 years. Lorman's presenters add that holders who disagree with an assessment face a very unclear administrative path, with most states lacking a clear appeal route, so disputes often end up in court rather than review [2TghvbJiOis @ 00:07:29]. Size does not save a holder either: most states let holders report de minimis items under $25 or $50 only in the aggregate, so dollar value is not an opportunity to skip reporting [2TghvbJiOis @ 00:16:51]. On the owner side, Money Missed relays FTC-flagged red flags: pressure like claim within 48 hours or forfeit it, upfront processing fees, demands for a full Social Security number before a claim starts, and law-firm letters about a distant relative's unclaimed life insurance [sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:11:42]. Any outreach script that resembles those patterns gets filed alongside the scams by the very claimants an agent is trying to convert.

callout.title: Kill Checks Before Chasing or Pitching a File
callout.body: Run these four checks before committing time, a fee agreement, or a claimant call. Each one is pulled from a pitfall a practitioner reported hitting or watching others hit.
items: Verify a real surplus survives second mortgages and liens before working any foreclosure file, and bring an attorney onto judicial and non-judicial mortgage cases [Money Making Juggernaut — 7WZONOtYbjc @ 00:05:15].

Never request payment before the claimant receives funds; a legitimate locator never asks to be paid first and fees sit around a 10% cap in most regulated states [Hoang Le CFP, EA, Real Estate Agent — kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:07:03].

Do not declare a zero result from a single state portal; state databases do not hold federal assets, so millions of searchers wrongly assume nothing is coming [This Guy Knows Tech — 74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:02:47].
Confirm the asset has cleared its dormancy period; an empty search may only mean the property has not yet been reported to the state [Hoang Le CFP, EA, Real Estate Agent — kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:02:14].

chapters.pull_quote: "The system moved without you. It usually does." — attributed to Base_Rate (RycXVSWGZ3I @ 00:03:42).
action_checklist: Run missingmoney.com first for a multi-state sweep, then use the unclaimed.org map for states running separate systems such as California and Pennsylvania (Money Missed, sfcrjWHv_7k @ 00:08:19).
Search every state lived in, worked in, or banked in, then rerun with maiden names, nicknames, and common misspellings (Unclaimed Money: Find What You're Owed, J4RhFyo0R7c @ 00:04:10).
Search deceased parents and grandparents by name, since property tied to them may legally belong to heirs, and search old business names (Hoang Le CFP, EA, Real Estate Agent, kZMkghcevh8 @ 00:04:24).

Sweep federal registries after state portals come back empty, including Department of Labor owed wages, PBGC, HUD FHA refunds, FDIC failed banks, and bankruptcy court funds (This Guy Knows Tech, 74IHdXzW4aQ @ 00:03:01).
For a lost 401K, pull the company's Form 5500 from the Department of Labor's lookup, which lists the plan administrator and phone number on the first page (InvestigateTV, YWsshlY3kF4 @ 00:01:36).
Recheck names and deceased loved ones' names at least once a year, because new property keeps getting reported (InvestigateTV, IhEPmIRt3Ak @ 00:03:02).

chapters.subtitle: State funds versus surplus funds, investigator roles, state selection, startup funding, beginner workflows, income examples, and reasons operators struggle or quit
chapters.executive_summary: State unclaimed funds operators agree the pool is enormous, estimated at 49 to 80-plus billion depending on the speaker, and that registration is usually a light lift of ID, paperwork, and sometimes a background check. The consensus launch order is: read the state's fee cap and claim-package rules, pick one niche and one or two states, set up a visible business footprint, and prospect daily with follow-up. Street mechanics center on downloading or buying state lists, filtering for big claims, with David Church refusing anything under 10,000 dollars at a 10% cap, skip tracing for free or roughly 14 to 15 dollars per 100 leads, loaded-opener scripts, and notarized agreements. The sharpest split is outreach: Wilkerson and Church lean on cold calls and follow-up, while Joe Green largely rejects cold calling and skip tracing for inbound social-media lead flow.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: A Deep Market, an Easy Door, and a Narrow Lane
paragraphs: Every operator here starts from the same premise: the money is real, it is massive, and it is not running out. David Church of Surplus Institute pegs the national pool at roughly 100 billion dollars, split about evenly between state unclaimed funds and mortgage and tax overages, then pulls a February 2023 figure showing states alone holding 70 billion, and tells anyone claiming the money is not there that they are lying [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:00:00] [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:01:21]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 puts state-level holdings above 80 billion and argues that volume is exactly what turns this into a predictable long-term career, because you will never run out of accounts to recover [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:01:28]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut defines the asset class cleanly: state funds are dormant savings accounts, uncashed checks, unclaimed insurance payouts, utility overpayments, PayPal balances, and death benefits that holders cannot keep and must turn over to the state treasurer, while surplus funds are foreclosure overages held at the county level [kuCEYN64vtQ @ 00:00:25]. The working consensus is that state funds are the simpler pitch, because the claimant already understands a forgotten bank account, and the operators who stay in the game treat that simplicity as their entry point rather than their ceiling.

The second point of agreement is that registration is easy and reading the state rules is mandatory. Timepiece Dan says becoming a state investigator means sending in your ID and answering a couple of questions, that anyone can become one, and that he believes the check exists mainly for tax purposes and to confirm who you are [sDutuuk5RG0 @ 00:02:06]. Wilkerson says most states do not require a license at all, only registration, and usually charge nothing; he tells newcomers to use the unclaimed.org map, click into a state, and line out three things before dialing anyone: what registration requires, how leads are obtained, and the exact claim package instructions, sometimes published as an investigator handbook [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:10:47]. Church runs the same drill live on the Mississippi treasury site, scrolling past the claim buttons to the FAQ, where he confirms the state works with claim finders at a maximum 10% fee before deciding it is workable [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:05:22]. Richardson frames the identical checkpoint for any market: before you pull a lead, know whether the state has stipulations on how you file a claim, how much you can charge, and any time duration, and understand that you do not have to live in the state you work [_vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:01:57].

The third consensus is that the people who wash out treat this as a lottery ticket, not a business. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO says the worst advice he got starting out was to just register and get going; with no website and no Google business footprint, claimants researched him and backed out of closed deals [XsLq9LUTb6w @ 00:01:05]. Green ties the backouts to trust: these people are not finding you, you are finding them, and they are handing over personal information. Green's six-step launch order starts by forcing beginners to pick one category, state funds or tax overages, because the filing process and the way you find people differ between them [i84F9CVghTA @ 00:01:03]. Wilkerson pushes the same narrowing even harder: one niche, then only one or two states, because the process is identical everywhere but each state's claim package quirks will stretch your mental bandwidth thin [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:04:19]. Church closes the loop on discipline, saying you may grind four to seven straight days with nothing before the yeses and call-me-back-tomorrows start, and that consistency is what eventually turns the light on [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:04:52]. Across all four, the baseline is the same: register, choose a lane, set a daily prospecting rhythm, and expect the first real results only after sustained volume.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Lists, Skip Tracing, Scripts, and the Claim Package
paragraphs: Lead sourcing differs sharply by state. Church downloads California's 500-and-up investigator file, opens the third file because it holds the highest claims, and warns that Mac Numbers choked on the data so he had to buy and download Excel [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:11:33]. Timepiece Dan scrolls the same California list live, counting close to 400,000 lines in just one of four files, and runs the math: a 30,000 dollar royalty claim at the 10% ceiling pays 3,000 [sDutuuk5RG0 @ 00:03:27]. Richardson says many states do not hand lists out free, quoting 25 dollars in Arkansas and 10 dollars in Massachusetts, and notes some states only offer an online portal where you run direct searches name by name [kuCEYN64vtQ @ 00:03:00]. When a state stays quiet, Church calls and asks for the list, and if the clerk asks why, he skips the heir-finder pitch and says it is public information, he is doing research, and he understands 70 billion sits unclaimed nationwide. States that refuse, he says, you simply cannot work [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:07:29].

Contact mechanics run from free to cheap, and every operator here builds them in the same order. Richardson's budget route is free TruePeopleSearch, with BeenVerified and Intelius as alternatives, while his volume shortcut is a batch skip tracing service where his promo code brings the cost to about 14 to 15 dollars per 100 leads, versus four, five, or even ten hours of manual research [_vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:02:55]. Timepiece Dan skips paid tools entirely and Googles the first name, last name, address, city, and state straight off the California list until numbers pop up, calling it the free way with no marketing spend [sDutuuk5RG0 @ 00:06:14]. The opener matters as much as the number. Church skips small talk; he loads the first line with the claimant's name, a former address, and the bank holding the dormant account, then says he is a licensed locator with the state and asks permission to retrieve the funds, a move he says stumbles the claimant into remembering the account [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:03:17]. Wilkerson treats delivery as theatrics, telling operators to read the script multiple times and then walk around the house rehearsing it, because how you react when someone says hello or hangs up matters almost more than the words themselves [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:13:30].

Closing the file is where state mechanics diverge most. Church says California pays the locator's 10% directly, so a 20,000 dollar check becomes 2,000 for him and 18,000 for the client, with no collecting from the client [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:01:43]. California also hands you its own two contracts, one notarized, and the package goes straight to the state, while other states make you assemble the contracts and information yourself, file with the state, and then collect your fee from the client after they are paid [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:03:55]. Wilkerson's rule of thumb is that most states require any claim agreement to be notarized once the account tops 1,000 dollars, some require it regardless, and nine times out of ten you will not get paid without it [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:15:44]. He sends the agreement and supporting documents to a notary near the claimant, who packages everything for the state, which he calls the most efficient way to run a transaction start to finish. Speed then depends on the treasury: Richardson says state funds typically process within 60 days because the check is literally already sitting in the State Treasury, unlike surplus funds that must clear a county legal review before payout [kuCEYN64vtQ @ 00:03:52].

callout.title: Small Edges That Separate Paid Operators from List Collectors
callout.body: These are the specific moves working operators use to get more contacts, more dollars per file, and access to states others write off.
items: Call on Saturdays and Sundays because contact rates run high, and cap the daily prospecting block at about a three-hour window, which Wilkerson treats as most people's mental limit for cold calling [Surplus Funds 101 — PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:05:58].

Run every surplus funds client through the state unclaimed property search as well; Richardson pulled 12,000 dollars more from the state treasury for one foreclosure client who had a forgotten savings account [Money Making Juggernaut — kuCEYN64vtQ @ 00:04:56].

In states like New York that only report claims as under or over 100 dollars, Church says if you work them at all, target Roth IRAs and IRA accounts because those carry the higher payouts [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:02:24].

For Florida, where you must work under a licensed party, Church is partnering with his tax overage lawyer on a 50/50 fee split and plans to push it toward 70/30 by feeding three or four claims a week [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:14:54].

sop_steps.title: Register and Map the State Rules
sop_steps.action: Pick one state, register as an investigator, and document registration, lead access, and claim package instructions.
sop_steps.detail: Use the unclaimed.org map to reach the state site, confirm whether a license or only registration is required, how leads are delivered, and the exact claim package the state expects; call the state if anything is unclear [Surplus Funds 101 — PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:10:47].

sop_steps.title: Pull and Filter the List
sop_steps.action: Download or request the state list and filter for claims large enough to justify the work at the state's cap.
sop_steps.detail: At a 10% cap, Church works nothing under 10,000 dollars and starts with a roughly 10,000 dollar claim; if no list is posted, he calls and asks for it as public information for research [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:07:42].

sop_steps.title: Skip Trace and Open the Call
sop_steps.action: Batch skip trace the filtered leads and open each call with the claimant's name, former address, and holder.
sop_steps.detail: Richardson's batch service runs about 14 to 15 dollars per 100 leads versus hours of manual research [Money Making Juggernaut — _vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:02:55]; Church's opener names the person, the address, and the dormant account, then asks permission to help retrieve the funds [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:03:17].

sop_steps.title: Paper, Notarize, and File the Claim Package
sop_steps.action: Fill out the state's agreement exactly as instructed, get it notarized near the claimant, and submit the full package.
sop_steps.detail: Wilkerson sends the agreement and supporting documents to a notary close to the claimant, who notarizes, packages everything, and usually ships it to the state, which he calls the most efficient way to run a transaction start to finish [Surplus Funds 101 — PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:17:08].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is how the first conversation happens. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO tells beginners to stop cold calling entirely, arguing nobody trusts a stranger delivering unbelievable news, and he labels skip tracing a waste of time while he closes deals with people who come to him through what he calls his Honeypot method [zI7m3acMjuY @ 00:00:15]. His build: drive people to a website or landing page form, research whoever submits, and even work small amounts pro bono in exchange for referrals, which he says flooded his inbox with brothers, sisters, parents and coworkers asking him to check for money [XsLq9LUTb6w @ 00:04:00]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 runs the opposite playbook: skip trace the state data and cold call, which he calls the quickest, cheapest, fastest way to gain traction, inside a three-hour daily prospecting window [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:12:49]. David Church of Surplus Institute backs the outbound route with a direct opener that names the person, a former address and the dormant Bank of America account before he pitches himself as a licensed locator asking permission to retrieve the funds [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:03:17]. Green concedes cold calling works for some, but says the other 98 percent with jobs and kids cannot dial six to eight hours a day.

Practitioners also split on what has to exist before the first dial. Joe Green treats funding as step one: file with the IRS and the state, open a business bank account, and ask for a 0 percent business credit card running 12 to 18 months, which he says carries 1 percent monthly minimums, can be pulled as a cash advance to pay yourself, and does not touch personal credit [i84F9CVghTA @ 00:06:13]. He also insists on a credibility footprint, because early prospects who researched him and found no website or Google business listing backed out of deals he had already closed [XsLq9LUTb6w @ 00:01:24]. David Wilkerson pushes the reverse mindset: kill the everything-has-to-be-perfect thinking, spend only on what produces revenue, and remember that his own first couple of deals closed before he even owned business cards [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:05:27]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut goes further and runs the full cycle for zero dollars with free county lists, free people-search skip tracing, his free call scenarios and self-typed service agreements, admitting the free route is inefficient and that you trade money for intelligence and time [sK5PqCLSzzg @ 00:03:56]. The real choice is whether credibility infrastructure and a funded runway come first, or raw dial volume on a shoestring.

State selection is the third fault line. David Church calls California pleasant because the state registers you and cuts your 10 percent check directly, so a $20,000 claim nets him $2,000 without chasing the client, though payouts can take six months or longer [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:01:43]. He avoids working Florida solo because of its investigator requirement, but his tax-overage lawyer offered a 50/50 fee split to work Florida state funds under the attorney, and Church plans to push that toward 70/30 by feeding three or four claims a week [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:15:11]. Timepiece Dan pitches California lists as the easy entry, scrolling past $12,000, $20,000 and $30,000 accounts and pricing a $30,000 claim at a $3,000 fee, noting the fee is negotiable up to the 10 percent ceiling [sDutuuk5RG0 @ 00:03:27]. Wilkerson walked away from California over its minimum six-month turnaround, ranks payout speed and bulk-lead access above fee size, points to Wisconsin and Michigan as faster payers, and leans toward 20 percent cap states because most states sit in the 10 to 20 percent band [qyRWV76TgwE @ 00:09:16]. Same state, opposite verdicts: one operator's easy entry is another's dead capital.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common failure the practitioners report is quitting before the pipeline matures. Joe Green says he has watched excited starters turn into a ghost town within two months because the business was more work than they expected and they never figured it out [Vy3iGS6ep4w @ 00:00:37]. David Wilkerson hears the same story from people who called their list one time, had one conversation, got no deal and wanted out; his rule is that today's work pays about three months down the road, so newcomers should lock in a six-month time frame [PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:09:12]. He also names state-hopping as a top killer: a beginner skip traces Florida leads, watches a guru pitch Utah, abandons the Florida pipeline, and eats the lost time, money and revenue [qyRWV76TgwE @ 00:04:08]. FundSleuth traces the quitting to a skills gap, reporting that course graduates who are excellent researchers get discouraged because their skip tracing source could not reach anyone or because they never learned to sell, since most courses do not coach the sales side, and even the hobbyist route of handing signed deals to a back-end partner demands research, skip tracing and closing skills [kGhoQfbhUG4 @ 00:04:11].

The second trap is bleeding personal money and credibility at the same time. Green says he burned his own cash and personal credit cards, slowed down the more he spent, and dialed hundreds of people a day from an unfamiliar out-of-area number while nobody picked up and those who did hung up mid-script [XsLq9LUTb6w @ 00:01:51]. He warns that pushing personal cards past 30 percent utilization drags your credit score down while you drain family money meant for bills [Vy3iGS6ep4w @ 00:01:22]. David Church faces a different leak: claimants who go around you and file directly after your call, which he says happens all the time and which he shrugs off because missing his weekly deal count matters far more than one lost claimant [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:09:55]. Wilkerson reports an internal leak, admitting that early on he subconsciously pushed deals away, including a claimant owed $50,000, because he did not feel he deserved to work a transaction that size [qyRWV76TgwE @ 00:05:20]. Each of these failures kills signed agreements rather than leads: the money is sitting on the list, but no ring, no trust or no nerve means no deal.

The economics checks are blunt. Under California's 10 percent cap, Church's $20,000 claim pays him $2,000 and the client $18,000, but one probate file took about eight months; New York only discloses whether an account is under or over $100, and Florida demands two years under a licensed investigator with fees capped at $1,000, so he refuses to work either state blind [IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:02:37]. His floor follows from the cap: nothing under $10,000, with a first claim sized around that mark [RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:07:42]. Eric Richardson adds that state lists are not always free, quoting $25 in Arkansas and $10 in Massachusetts, and he expects state claims to process within 60 days because the money already sits in the treasury, a timeline that collides with the multi-month California waits Church and Wilkerson describe [kuCEYN64vtQ @ 00:02:47]. Joe Green's volume check: if ten calls a day yields one pickup and doubling to twenty still yields one, more dialing is wasted energy, and you only learn that by tracking the ratio for two to three weeks instead of guessing [i84F9CVghTA @ 00:10:08].

callout.title: Clear These Four Gates Before Scaling Dial Volume
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a pipeline the practitioners watched break; clear all four before buying more data or adding callers.
items: Do not dial until you have pulled the state's registration requirements, fee cap, agreement form and claim-package instructions, and call the state office if anything is unclear [Surplus Funds 101 — PGvJEv9Y_Go @ 00:11:19].
Commit to three to five follow-up calls per prospect, because most competitors never make a second call [Surplus Funds 101 — qyRWV76TgwE @ 00:08:00].
Track calls-to-pickups for two to three weeks before doubling volume, so you do not cut the channel that actually works [Unclaimed CEO — i84F9CVghTA @ 00:09:25].

Skip claims you cannot size: avoid states that only report under or over $100 unless chasing IRA or Roth accounts, and hold a $10,000 floor under a 10 percent cap [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — IIBKDdChS-k @ 00:02:24].

chapters.pull_quote: "It's not really about the state that you choose to work in, it's how you work the state." — Surplus Funds 101 (qyRWV76TgwE @ 00:08:40).
action_checklist: Pick one category, state funds or tax overages, and work only one or two states until deals flow [Unclaimed CEO — i84F9CVghTA @ 00:00:48].

Call the state unclaimed property office, ask for its list, and if asked why, say it is public information you are researching [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — RjCjrBjQF7Y @ 00:07:29].

chapters.question_prompt: How can operators evaluate public search resources and understand the state custody and return practices that affect owners?
chapters.title: Public Portals and State Return Practices
chapters.subtitle: MissingMoney.com, free government searches, Delaware search resources and revenue practices, automatic checks, California account-transfer cases, and efforts to improve returns
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree that states hold escheated money as custodians, the owner's claim never dies, and official search and claiming cost nothing. MissingMoney.com, run under the state administrators' association, is the consensus first sweep. Each state portal where the owner lived, worked, or rented comes next, searched under name variants, business names, and deceased relatives. The street mechanics are concrete: result pages of 20, 40, or 80, info-versus-claim routing, Delaware's over-50 and under-50 bands, logged claim numbers, Social Security and proof-of-address demands, and a Delaware check reported within two weeks. Return practice splits sharply. Illinois mailed 140,000 checks worth $13.2 million, and New York auto-mails claims of $250 or less. California waits for owners to file on $7 billion across 28 million accounts. Finders can take up to half.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same baseline. When a holder loses contact with an owner past the dormancy window, the money is escheated to a state, and the state holds it as a keeper, not an owner. The Explainer Point lays it out flatly: every state and the District of Columbia runs a program, the owner never loses the right to ask for the money back, and states charge no fee to search or to claim [NWkWT5QX3sM @ 00:00:54]. Off The Receipt describes the same handoff. The business, which the law calls the holder, must report the money and turn it over once the dormancy clock runs out, and the state holds it as custodian against any future claim [hSrCCZHDpUU @ 00:01:07]. Lunch Cash supplies the timing operators plan around: the waiting period is often 3 to 5 years before a company must hand the money to the state, and the owner can still claim it years later [R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:01:00]. The payment rule is just as unanimous. Nobody Asked, I Checked tells searchers that any site demanding payment before it shows results is off the official path. Penelope Jane Smith is blunter: you never have to pay to reclaim your money, so anyone asking for cash to unlock or register funds should be deleted and blocked [z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:02:54] [26FSCbZczh4 @ 00:01:55].

The second point of agreement is search breadth. Companies send lost-account funds to the state of the owner's last known address. Penelope Jane Smith's rule follows from that: search every state you have lived in, run the same sweep for family members who have passed, and circle back about once a year because records change [26FSCbZczh4 @ 00:03:43]. FundForge widens the net to every state where you have lived, worked, or rented an apartment, plus relatives' names, and notes that most states set no claim deadline, so there is no reason to panic [hPHajccTyH0 @ 00:11:37]. Nobody Asked, I Checked adds a name-variation layer: full legal name, any old married name, and common misspellings. A small change can make a record appear or vanish, and a re-run a year later catches the new reports businesses file with states every year [z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:01:45]. On tooling, the consensus lands on MissingMoney.com. Jordan Liles, a reporter who mostly covers scams, went in expecting this to be one. He concluded it was legit after finding holder names, addresses, and amount bands organized in a way he says lazy scammers would never bother to build. He then confirmed through Google News coverage that the site is endorsed by the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators and the National Association of State Treasurers [lM8PdIOG7-E @ 00:02:31].

Practitioners converge most sharply on the gap between states that push money out and states that wait for owners to file. In Illinois, Treasurer Michael Frerichs mailed checks to 140,000 residents in a single week, totaling $13.2 million against roughly $5 billion held. His staff first cross-checked owners against other state databases, and he publicly told recipients the envelope is not a scam [4abzayS6yzk @ 00:00:17]. New York's Comptroller now verifies ownership and mails checks for claims of $250 or less without any filing, under a law signed by Governor Kathy Hochul, while paying out $1.5 million a day from a $19 billion account [wCk_H4rThTo @ 00:00:38]. California sits at the other pole. CBS News California found that the state does not automatically return money to people, nonprofits, or small businesses, even though unclaimed property generates about a billion dollars a year for its general fund and the state keeps the interest [1Grj5UvPLwo @ 00:00:30]. The Legislative Analyst's Office named the structural problem directly: when property owners do not benefit, the state does, so there is always a built-in tension. Ryan Miller's analysis recommended automatic returns so some owners would never have to file a claim [0xrXfpILRzI @ 00:01:38].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On MissingMoney.com the run is mechanical. Knowledge Work Nexus types a personal name, then repeats the search under every business name or alternate name ever used. Results page in sets of 20, 40, or 80, and a thousand-hit list takes a few minutes to scan because results cannot be sorted by state [wO5QkFr7vdQ @ 00:01:08]. The presenter knew one record was theirs because the address matched their best friend Gail's former home. Clicking claim drops the item into a cart, and the view claimed properties button at the top of the list opens a relationship selector: owner or several other roles. Then come the form, a signature, a review, and a submission that returns a claim number [wO5QkFr7vdQ @ 00:02:23]. Mike Bogdan of Financial Soup ran John Jones across all states with no city, pulled over a thousand properties, and showed the two buttons on each result. Info routes to the holding state's official site, while claim uses the cart [ubLk2A5a-2A @ 00:02:36]. Bogdan prefers the info route and files directly through the state. He notes that not every state subscribes to in-site claiming, so for some records you have to use info and file with that state's treasury department [ubLk2A5a-2A @ 00:03:29].

Direct state portals follow the same skeleton with tighter fields. Michael Curtis of forgottenloot.org walks through Delaware's official site. You enter a first and last name, just a last name, or a property ID if one arrived in a mailer, a newspaper notice, or an event handout. A common name returns 1,000 records [JGravBgJTJo @ 00:02:58]. Delaware shows over-50 and under-50 bands rather than exact figures. You pick a record, hit view claim, act as owner, fill every red-asterisk field, answer the how-did-you-hear menu, preview, and write down the claim number from the summary [JGravBgJTJo @ 00:04:06]. Curtis says he did not believe it until a check arrived within two weeks of filing, and the site banner claims over $300 million returned in three years. KFNETWORK searched Kim Davis and added a city to narrow the popular name. They call the over-50 and under-50 bands not transparent and note that other states show exact dollar amounts [0anLNGLjnlA @ 00:03:04]. The form then asks for a Social Security number and phone number, and the follow-up email may request copies of Social Security documents, a birth certificate, and proof of address. Heirs pick the heir relationship instead of owner [0anLNGLjnlA @ 00:04:22].

Verification and cost control are where the numbers live. Jordan Liles checks a portal by searching its domain in quotes on Google News, not regular Google. He then reads whether outlets like Good Morning America, CNET, and local affiliates tie the site to state programs. That route showed MissingMoney.com covering 41 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and Alberta [lM8PdIOG7-E @ 00:03:18]. Bogdan's due-diligence stack has four parts: a whois lookup on the domain, a Google search of the domain plus the word complaint, a look at Reddit threads, and asking ChatGPT how the site is monetized [ubLk2A5a-2A @ 00:01:53]. Nobody Asked, I Checked puts the finder math on the table. Wyoming's treasurer warned that private finders can take up to half of what they recover. The channel's log records the name searched, the state, the amount, the claim number, and the date, so claims in two states never get mixed up [z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:04:59]. Lunch Cash tells searchers to type the MissingMoney address directly, because ads can lead to look-alike sites [R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:08:06]. Delaware's law also limits what finders can charge and bans finder deals entirely for the first two years after the money reaches the state [R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:08:43].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The deepest split in state practice is whether the treasury mails the money out or waits for the owner to come hunting. Illinois Treasurer Michael Frerichs sent checks to 140,000 residents over the last week after staff double-checked holdings against other state databases to confirm rightful owners, and Frerichs told recipients the envelope is not a scam and to simply cash it [4abzayS6yzk @ 00:00:34]. New York now runs the same play by statute: for any claim of $250 or less, the Comptroller's office verifies ownership and mails the check instead of just sending a notice, under a law signed by Governor Kathy Hochul [wCk_H4rThTo @ 00:00:38]. California is the counter-example. CBS News California found the state does not automatically return money to people, nonprofits, or small businesses, even with Children's Hospital owed $1.3 million and food banks sitting in the database [1Grj5UvPLwo @ 00:00:30]. Delaware lands in between: Lunch Cash reports the state returns $150 million to $200 million a year on average and sends some money back automatically, without a filed claim, to taxpayers it can match [R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:03:50]. For an operator, home-state rules decide whether a dormant balance arrives in the mailbox unprompted or surfaces only when someone runs the search.

Practitioners also split on how to treat unexpected contact and which button to press once a match appears. Penelope Jane Smith teaches that, to their knowledge, U.S. unclaimed property offices do not reach out to owners, and that anyone who contacts you needing money to unlock or register a balance should be deleted and blocked [26FSCbZczh4 @ 00:01:55]. Nobody Asked, I Checked takes a more surgical line on a letter about money you do not recognize: do not assume it is a scam, do not assume it is real, and look up the holder name and amount in the state's official search before acting [z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:06:37]. On MissingMoney.com the routes diverge again. Mike Bogdan of Financial Soup shows the site offers an Info button that sends you to the state's official site and a Claim button that builds a cart, then admits having no experience with the cart and claiming only through the state route [ubLk2A5a-2A @ 00:03:09]. Knowledge Work Nexus ran the cart route live, chose the owner relationship, signed, submitted, and got a claim number on the spot, while still stressing that every state runs its own process behind the portal [wO5QkFr7vdQ @ 00:02:45].

Even the headline numbers practitioners use to sell the search do not line up across channels, so an operator quoting them to a client should name the source. Penelope Jane Smith puts the national pile at about $33 billion and relays NAUPA's figure that about 1 in 10 people have unclaimed property, defined as accounts with no activity or owner contact for over a year [26FSCbZczh4 @ 00:02:37]. The Explainer Point uses roughly $70 billion held, one in seven Americans affected, an average claim of about $2,000, about $4.5 billion returned in the 12 months ending June 2024, and states charging no fee to search or claim [NWkWT5QX3sM @ 00:01:13]. Delaware's own homepage figures shift too. sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure practitioners documented is not a lost check but a liquidated position. CBS News Sacramento reported a retired couple whose $275,000 investment account showed zeros after the owner went three years without touching it or having any contact, at which point the state required Schwab to transfer the holdings into California's program [80djyAsS-YE @ 00:00:35]. The state then blamed Schwab for errors in the transfer while Schwab pointed the owner back to the state [80djyAsS-YE @ 00:01:02], and although the couple eventually claimed all of the property, the owner called the program a disgrace. The deeper hit comes after the sale. CBS News California reports state law requires California to cash out stocks and investments within 20 months of receiving them, so the owner collects whatever they sold for, not what the position is worth on the day of the claim [1Grj5UvPLwo @ 00:02:52]. The Explainer Point walks through Colette Barf's 2024 suit: Microsoft shares sent to Delaware in 2015 after a letter went to an address in South Africa, sold for nearly $200,000, and worth almost $2 million by the time of the lawsuit [NWkWT5QX3sM @ 00:06:47].

The scam surface is wide, and practitioners mapped it from both directions. Nobody Asked, I Checked relays Wyoming's treasurer warning that private finders can take up to half of what they recover while the state charges nothing, plus Oklahoma's treasurer flagging a site that charges a monthly fee to search records the official site always shows for free [z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:05:15]. Lunch Cash tells searchers to type MissingMoney.com in by hand because ads can lead to look-alike sites, and to check their own state's official site as well [R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:08:06]. KFNETWORK's own origin story shows the trap and the escape in one move: in 2017, while job hunting online in Missouri, they clicked an ad promising unclaimed state money, worked through the prompts, and only trusted it after an email supplied a number to call the state directly [0anLNGLjnlA @ 00:01:11]. Penelope Jane Smith warns that even a claimed government endorsement can be fishy, so always validate before clicking [26FSCbZczh4 @ 00:05:57]. Across these operators the screen is identical: free search, a government domain, no upfront fee, and an independently confirmed phone number before any personal data changes hands.

Owner-side unit economics are mostly small tickets with real paperwork friction. Jordan Liles, who went in expecting a scam, warns that finding millions from a distant relative is too good to be true and points instead to forgotten prepaid cards near $25 or a clinic refund around $150 [lM8PdIOG7-E @ 00:04:00]. CBS News Sacramento's street test turned up $70 owed to Jody Cole from State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance, pulled from 38,000 Cole results in California alone [0xrXfpILRzI @ 00:00:49]. Friction scales with name frequency: Knowledge Work Nexus hit a thousand results, could not sort them by state, and only spotted a real match because it carried a best friend's former address [wO5QkFr7vdQ @ 00:01:29]. On the holder side, the downside is far steeper. FundForge reports that in the Temple Inland audit, with complete files surviving only back to about 2003, Kelmar's estimation produced a first assessment of $2.1 million while only $147.30 of actual property was identified [hPHajccTyH0 @ 00:05:54]. The same channel's fix for holders is blunt: good records matter most, because without them an auditor may estimate, and estimates can be large.

callout.title: Stop Before You File, Pay, or Leave an Account Idle
callout.body: Every gate below traces to a loss, a near miss, or a scam pattern practitioners reported firsthand. Clear all four before submitting personal data or letting a holder escheat an investment position.
items: Never pay anyone to see or release a balance; the state does not charge to give you your own money back, and an upfront fee is a red flag [Lunch Cash — R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:08:43].
Verify any unexpected letter or check by looking up the holder name and amount in the state's official search before acting on it [Nobody Asked, I Checked — z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:06:37].
Write down the claim number the moment it appears so you can refer to it later when the state follows up [Michael Curtis — JGravBgJTJo @ 00:05:29].
Keep brokerage and bank accounts active, because even a small transaction or a call to the bank can restart the dormancy clock before a forced transfer [FundForge — hPHajccTyH0 @ 00:12:12].

chapters.pull_quote: "Nobody needs a fee to show you your money, and nobody should ask you to pay before your own name shows up in a database." — Nobody Asked, I Checked (z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:09:09).
action_checklist: Run the four-step plan in one sitting: search your own state's office, run the multistate search, check the federal databases that fit your situation, and save every claim number and office name [Nobody Asked, I Checked — z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:08:03].

Search your full legal name plus any old married name and common misspellings, because records can list a name differently and a small change can make a result appear or vanish [Nobody Asked, I Checked — z2nZM27w4qU @ 00:01:26].
Search every state where you have lived, worked, or rented an apartment, and search relatives' names too, because you can look for funds that belong to family [FundForge — hPHajccTyH0 @ 00:11:37].
Type MissingMoney.com in yourself instead of clicking ads, then also check your own state's official site and any state you have lived in [Lunch Cash — R6nRcAkxVdA @ 00:08:06].
Search under any business name you operated as well as your personal name, and narrow common names by adding a city [KFNETWORK — 0anLNGLjnlA @ 00:02:39].

For a deceased relative's property, select the heir relationship and be ready for an email requesting copies of Social Security card, birth certificate, and proof of address [KFNETWORK — 0anLNGLjnlA @ 00:03:43].

chapters.question_prompt: How do the demonstrated state searches locate personal unclaimed property and forgotten utility deposits?
chapters.title: State-by-State Personal Property Searches
chapters.subtitle: Texas, Pennsylvania, New York, Georgia, and Massachusetts search walkthroughs; utility-deposit searches in Iowa, Montana, Colorado, Kansas, and Maryland
chapters.executive_summary: State unclaimed property portals across Texas, New York, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Indiana, Iowa, Montana, Colorado, Kansas, Maryland and Georgia run on the same engine: holders remit dormant money after losing contact, the state holds it, and you pull it back with a last-name search plus ID and address proof. Practitioners agree the search is free, name variations and old addresses unlock hidden records, and paid finders run the identical database. Street numbers: Texas averages 37 business days, New York pays most simple claims within 30 days, Colorado's average claim is $918, and utility deposits escheat after one year in Iowa, Montana and Kansas. They split on finder fee ceilings (15% in New York and Kansas, 10% to 30% in Georgia, 10% to 40% in Montana), on whether amounts are shown, and on how long states hold funds.

key_metrics.label: Texas Average Claim Turnaround
key_metrics.value: 37 business days
key_metrics.context: WFAA reports the Texas Comptroller's office said last year's average turnaround for all claim types was 37 business days, with heirship claims taking longer and missing documentation slowing payouts.

key_metrics.label: New York Finder Fee Cap
key_metrics.value: 15% of recovered funds, written notarized contract required
key_metrics.context: Location service providers are capped at 15% under Abandoned Property Law Section 1416; the state sends 100% of the check to the owner, who then pays the provider.

key_metrics.label: Colorado Average Claim Payout
key_metrics.context: The Great Colorado Payback holds over $700 million across over a million individual properties, with the average claim paying out $918.

key_metrics.label: Montana Automatic Payout Ceiling
key_metrics.value: Up to $1,000 without a formal claim
key_metrics.context: House Bill 88 from the 2025 session lets the Department of Revenue match and mail up to $1,000 using state tax records; manual searching is still encouraged for records that do not auto-match.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Nearly every speaker frames the state as a custodian, not a confiscator. KHOU 11 reports that by law businesses and financial institutions must turn money over to the state once they lose contact with the owner, and the Texas Comptroller is holding more than $10 billion [uY7XnXFfpv4 @ 00:00:18]. Как се прави pins New York's trigger at roughly three years without owner-directed activity, after which the holder runs a due diligence attempt to reach you and then remits, with the state holding the funds in perpetual custody and no statute of limitations, so money lost three years or thirty years ago is equally claimable [cF0HhlLh7NI @ 00:02:26]. GardenShop.Pro repeats the model for Kansas, describing the state as a perpetual safekeeper with no maintenance fees draining balances and no forfeiture [E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:02:00]. The inventory is consistent: forgotten bank accounts, uncashed checks, utility deposits, insurance refunds, final paychecks, gift cards, stock dividends and safe deposit box contents. NBC New York adds that the money is usually uncashed checks sent to an old address, reported by banks, retailers and health insurers [qHskTBuAHTg @ 00:00:35]. The operator takeaway: anything a business owed you and could not deliver sits in a state ledger, indexed by the name and address that business had on file.

The second consensus point is that the search itself is a last-name game, and exact-match indexing punishes lazy queries. Как се прави tells New York searchers to start with the surname or business name, refine with first name, city or zip, and then grind through maiden names, common misspellings and previous addresses, because even a tiny typo in how a bank recorded your name years ago can hide a match [9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:02:54]. GardenShop.Pro pushes this harder for utility money in Iowa: accounts are recorded under the exact name given when the account was opened, so if the gas company misspelled your name a decade ago you have to search that exact typo [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:04:13]. The same channel's Maryland walkthrough says utilities logged names exactly as they appeared on the paper contract, so test hyphenated and unhyphenated versions, maiden names, and any LLC or small business name the bill ran under [1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:04:31]. NBC New York gives the same instruction in one line: if your name is often misspelled, check the list for misspellings [qHskTBuAHTg @ 00:01:24]. Geography is the other lever. The money is tied to the address the holder had, not where you live now, so old cities and zip codes are filters to work, not afterthoughts.

Third, every practitioner who addresses fees says the state route is free and the paid route duplicates it. Как се прави warns that location service providers mail letters offering to recover your money for a percentage, and says flatly that they are simply running a last name search on the exact same free public database, while going direct keeps 100% of the recovered funds [cF0HhlLh7NI @ 00:06:41]. GardenShop.Pro's Montana breakdown puts the ask at 10% to 40% of the deposit and lands on the same verdict: they are searching the same free database you now know how to use [3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:07:21]. The consensus also extends the hunt beyond your own name and your own state. WFAA tells viewers to search the names of friends and family while on the Texas portal and to hit the unclaimed property site for every state they have previously lived in [0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:01:59]. GardenShop.Pro's Georgia episode goes further, noting the database is public and free to search, so you can look up parents, siblings, friends, and even current or former employers, then call them with the find [DVmNNFdoDzE @ 00:07:34]. That network search is where the volume lives: one name is one shot, while a family tree crossed with every former address and state multiplies the number of shots you get at a hit.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Portals differ sharply in what they show you before you file, and that dictates how you triage results. On the Texas portal, WFAA reports that claimable property appears with the dollar amount listed [0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:00:17], and KHOU 11 shows the claim page naming the exact amount and type, down to contents of a safety deposit box [uY7XnXFfpv4 @ 00:00:48]. Pennsylvania runs a color-coded grid. Michael Curtis walks through it: green rows mean you must contact the office to determine eligibility, white rows are single-owner records you can claim, gray rows are joint ownership, and each row shows the reporting company with amounts only bucketed as under 100 or over 100 [0YK26E_fzYA @ 00:03:35]. He notes an over-100 record could be $500 or more and you simply do not know until you request the claim form, and that the results grid shows only the first 400 rows. Maryland, per GardenShop.Pro, uses prefix matching, so a search for Doe finds Doe, John but can miss a record filed as Estate of John Doe because the first word is Estate [1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:03:58]. Anyone working a deceased relative's money needs to search with the estate prefix as well as the surname, and anyone working Pennsylvania should narrow with city and address before hitting that 400-row ceiling.

Filing follows the same skeleton everywhere: claim button, relationship to owner, identity fields, then documents. WFAA lays out Texas click by click: hit claim next to the listing, open view claimed properties, pick your relationship from the dropdown as owner, heir or trustee, enter name, address and Social Security number, confirm you are telling the truth and submit; the state then sends a claim listing the items it needs, such as a driver's license and documents showing your relationship to the property [0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:00:50]. In Iowa, GardenShop.Pro says a web wizard asks for current mailing address, phone and legal relationship, then emails a unique claim ID for tracking; minimum paperwork is a signed claim form, photo ID and Social Security number, plus historic address proof like an old lease [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:03:40]. Maryland adds form COT ST-912, which must be notarized if the claim is over $500, with portal upload as the fastest path or mail to Baltimore [1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:05:32]. Kansas splits the channels: routine ID and mail scans go through digital upload, but an original certified death certificate or notarized affidavit of heirship cannot be emailed or faxed and must be mailed to the division in Topeka [E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:06:00].

Turnaround numbers are specific and swing with claim complexity. WFAA reports the Texas Comptroller's average turnaround last year was 37 business days across all claim types, with heirship claims running longer and incomplete documentation slowing things down [0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:01:42]. Как се прави gives New York's clock: a confirmation email within 48 hours, processing within 30 days if no further action is needed, and up to 90 days if the state asks for ID or proof of an old address; the check then arrives in a perforated envelope and must be cashed by December 31 of the following calendar year or it goes abandoned again [9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:03:36]. GardenShop.Pro tiers Colorado: simple cash claims with clear address matches in a few days to about four weeks, manual address validation in 90 to 150 days, and heirship, probate or business claims commonly six to twelve months [GWa4tWyuEoA @ 00:06:02]. The same channel flags the haircut the quick news segments skip: in Montana, approved claims are cross-referenced against government debts, so delinquent state taxes, unpaid child support, IRS assessments or tribal court obligations come out first and you receive a paper warrant check for the net balance [3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:06:37].

callout.title: Index Hacks That Surface Buried Records
callout.body: The practitioners keep returning to one idea: the database matches what the holder typed, so you search the way the holder recorded you, not the way you spell yourself.
items: Search the holder's typo, not your name: utility accounts are recorded under the exact name given at signup, so a misspelling from a decade ago is the only query that finds it [GardenShop.Pro — OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:04:13].
Run the estate prefix as a separate search on Maryland's portal, because prefix matching misses records filed as Estate of John Doe when you only type Doe [GardenShop.Pro — 1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:03:58].

In Colorado, electric and gas deposits never reach the state portal; call the provider directly, such as Xcel Energy at 1-800-895-4999, with the former service address, dates and Social Security number ready [GardenShop.Pro — GWa4tWyuEoA @ 00:03:32].
On Pennsylvania's claim form, Social Security number and date of birth carry no red asterisk, but entering them if you know them speeds the claim up [Michael Curtis — 0YK26E_fzYA @ 00:07:28].

sop_steps.action: List legal surname, maiden and prior married names, nicknames, hyphenated forms, misspellings, business names, and every former address.

sop_steps.title: Run each state portal plus the national registry
sop_steps.action: Search the official portal for every state you lived in, then run missingmoney.com for cross-state holders.
sop_steps.detail: Kansas searchers start at missingmoney.ks.gov and also run missingmoney.com, especially after living in multiple states, typing just the last name and then variations [GardenShop.Pro — E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:03:21].

sop_steps.action: Match name and old address, read the property type and holder, then hit claim and select your relationship to the owner.
sop_steps.detail: Click claim next to the listing, open view claimed properties, choose owner, heir or trustee from the dropdown, then enter name, address and Social Security number and submit [WFAA — 0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:00:33].

sop_steps.action: Assemble photo ID, Social Security proof, current address proof, and documentation tying you to the prior address before submitting.
