sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split runs through third-party finders. Как се прави, in its New York explainer, treats location service providers as a regulated lane rather than a scam: their fee is capped at a maximum of 15% of recovered funds, they need a written notarized contract, and the state still mails 100% of the check to the owner, leaving the owner to pay the provider afterward [9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:05:12]. The same channel's last-name walkthrough takes the hard line instead. If a finder letter shows up offering recovery for a percentage, do not pay, because the finder is simply running a last-name search on the identical free public database [cF0HhlLh7NI @ 00:06:28]. GardenShop.Pro adds a timing weapon from Iowa: any agreement to pay a finder made within the first 24 months of the state holding the property is unenforceable, and after that window the fee is still capped at 15% with a strict notarized contract [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:05:17]. In Georgia, the same channel concedes that claimants designated representatives operate legally and can charge 10 to 30%, then runs the math: a $1,000 find means handing over $300 for a search the owner could run free [DVmNNFdoDzE @ 00:04:19]. Both camps agree the state itself never takes a cut.

Operators also split on how wide to throw the first search. Michael Curtis, working Pennsylvania's treasury database, pushes narrowing: last name, first name, middle initial, city, and the old address if it is known, because without those fields the operator faces a long list to scroll through [0YK26E_fzYA @ 00:11:35]. Как се прави argues the reverse for New York. Start broad, keep geographic filters wide, and never lock the first pass to the current zip code, because money left behind after a move is tied to the old address; a reporter pulled two claims linked to former addresses in Queens and Albany exactly that way [cF0HhlLh7NI @ 00:04:25]. GardenShop.Pro's Maryland walkthrough explains why simple input beats detailed input on some portals: claimitmd.gov runs a prefix matching algorithm, so a plain 'Doe' surfaces 'Doe, John' but can miss a record filed as 'Estate of John Doe' because the first word is Estate [1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:03:42]. What comes back on screen differs too. KHOU 11 showed the Texas portal listing the exact amount and the kind of money, down to the contents of a safety deposit box [uY7XnXFfpv4 @ 00:00:48], while Pennsylvania only bands rows as under or over 100 and Maryland hides exact figures until identity is proven.

States also disagree on whether the owner has to lift a finger at all. GardenShop.Pro reports that Iowa's Money Match program cross-references the unclaimed property database against current state income tax filings and mails a check automatically, no claim form required [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:04:46]. Montana's House Bill 88, passed in the 2025 legislative session, lets the Department of Revenue match and pay out up to $1,000 using state tax records, yet the same walkthrough still pushes manual searching because the auto-pay feature has limits and will not trigger on everything [3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:02:43]. Colorado runs a similar automated identification match against state tax and motor vehicle records, and if one of those checks shows up in the mail the owner can cash it right away [GWa4tWyuEoA @ 00:04:04]. The holding clock is the other fault line. New York, Kansas, Maryland, and Georgia are all described as perpetual custodians with no deadline, but Indiana's attorney general told WTHR his office keeps unclaimed money for 25 years, after which it goes to the state, which is why Indiana set up a booth at the state fair so people walking by could run a quick search [pPow2SwrxBE @ 00:01:16]. For Indiana claimants, waiting carries a real cost rather than a safe default.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive mistake reported is an incomplete file. GardenShop.Pro's Montana walkthrough calls it the most common reason claimants hit a frustrating 6-month claim denial, and the fix is to gather a government-issued photo ID, Social Security proof, current address proof, and documentation of the prior address tied to the property before hitting submit; a Missoula rental from 10 years ago has to be proven [3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:06:08]. WFAA heard that the Texas document request 'can be a pain,' with the state asking for a driver's license or supporting documentation showing the claimant's relationship to the property, and when an old utility bill is missing, most companies will hand over a copy [0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:01:10]. Delivery-channel rules trip people next. GardenShop.Pro warns that Kansas will not take an original certified death certificate or a notarized affidavit of heirship by email or fax; those have to travel by physical mail to the unclaimed property division in Topeka [E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:06:00]. Maryland's form COT ST-912 must be notarized once the claim tops $500, and the checklist adds a historical lease, a bank record from that year, or an old utility statement proving residence at the BGE or Pepco service address [1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:05:32].

Approval does not mean the full amount lands. GardenShop.Pro describes Montana's interagency revenue offsets: once a claim is approved, the state must cross-reference the claimant against outstanding government debts, so delinquent state taxes, unpaid child support, IRS assessments, or tribal court obligations come out of the deposit first, followed by a written explanation and a paper warrant check for the net balance [3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:06:37]. Kansas runs the same play through its mandatory setoff program, checking a centralized state debt database and intercepting delinquent income taxes, child support, and district court fines before the treasurer writes the check; only a refund larger than the debt pays out, and only the net [E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:07:00]. The second leak is sitting on the check. Как се прави says New York owners generally have until December 31st of the following calendar year to cash it, or the funds become abandoned all over again and the whole claim restarts from scratch; property that was originally interest-bearing may also be subject to federal and state taxes [9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:05:56]. Iowa's Money Match envelope arrives looking like junk mail, and GardenShop.Pro warns against throwing it away, because it has to be cashed within 6 months [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:05:01].

Search-side traps cost just as much. GardenShop.Pro stresses that utility accounts are recorded under the exact name given when the account was created, so a decade-old gas company misspelling has to be searched as that exact typo, along with maiden, hyphenated, and other spelling variations [OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:04:13]. Pennsylvania's results grid hides its own trap: Michael Curtis shows that green rows mean the claimant must contact the office to determine eligibility, white rows are single-owner records that can be claimed directly, and gray rows mark joint ownership [0YK26E_fzYA @ 00:03:14]. On the fraud side, WTHR's Indiana segment warns to make sure the search runs on the right official website and nothing else, because the government will not charge a fee to recover your own money [pPow2SwrxBE @ 00:01:33]. Как се прави lists the red flags in detail: anyone demanding an upfront fee, an administrative charge, or a made-up clearance tax; unsolicited text messages or cold calls asking for a full Social Security number or bank passwords; and pressure claiming the money is about to be permanently forfeited to the government [9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:04:47]. Every one of these warnings collapses into the same discipline: official portal only, the exact name on the old account, and no money paid up front.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Claim Goes Out the Door
callout.body: These gates come straight from the delays, denials, and payout leaks practitioners hit on real state portals. Clear all four before filing or cashing.
items: Assemble photo ID, Social Security proof, current address proof, and prior-address documentation before submitting, because an incomplete file is the most common trigger for a 6-month claim denial [GardenShop.Pro — 3iluxKs2wP8 @ 00:06:08].
Price in setoffs before counting the money: Kansas intercepts delinquent state income taxes, child support, and court fines and only pays the net balance [GardenShop.Pro — E2EtkM2OBvI @ 00:07:00].
Cash the state check promptly; in New York the deadline is generally December 31st of the following calendar year or the funds go abandoned again [Как се прави — 9BVp_yhswZY @ 00:05:56].
Confirm the official state URL and refuse any upfront fee, because the government will not charge a fee to recover your own money [WTHR — pPow2SwrxBE @ 00:01:33].

chapters.pull_quote: "I tell folks all the time, if you lost parents or grandparents you could be entitled to the money. It goes back to the 1940s." - NBC New York (qHskTBuAHTg @ 00:00:51).
action_checklist: Run the unclaimed property search on the official website of every state you have previously lived in, plus the names of friends and family members [WFAA — 0UUN2j2_dFU @ 00:01:59].
If your name is often misspelled, check the list for misspellings and also search relatives, including those who have passed on [NBC New York — qHskTBuAHTg @ 00:01:10].
On Iowa results, isolate category codes UT01 for deposits and UT02 for refunds to confirm a utility deposit hit before filing [GardenShop.Pro — OFnbGkVuoHQ @ 00:02:52].
Run a multi-state search on missingmoney.com when a utility parent company was incorporated elsewhere or you moved across state lines [GardenShop.Pro — 1IpkVjkkXHg @ 00:08:04].
After finding your name in Texas, hit claim, fill out the application, and track the claim's progress online at no cost [KHOU 11 — WdhaqcAUXBk @ 00:00:55].

In Pennsylvania, pick a white single-owner row, request the claim form, complete every red-asterisk field, and add optional SSN and birth date to speed processing [Michael Curtis — 0YK26E_fzYA @ 00:07:06].

chapters.question_prompt: How can an operator search for unclaimed funds belonging to corporations and other businesses across the states demonstrated?
chapters.title: Find Unclaimed Funds Under Business Names
chapters.subtitle: Corporate-name searches and state walkthroughs for Tennessee, Virginia, Missouri, North Dakota, Colorado, South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Connecticut, Georgia, Rhode Island, and Oklahoma
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners hunting business-name unclaimed funds agree on one core truth: the money sits in perpetual state custody, the search is free, and most misses come from searching wrong. Как се прави walkthroughs in North Dakota, Minnesota, South Carolina and Oklahoma hammer the same portal trap: put the company in the last-name field and leave first name blank, or commercial records vanish. Every operator stacks name variants (DBAs, truncations, dropped suffixes, acquired entities, old zip codes) and backs claims with FEIN proof, officer authority and a historical-address link. Numbers run from Colorado's 10 MB, five-file upload rules and 6 to 12 month merger cycles to Georgia's 10% agent cap versus 30% CDR cap. The sharpest split: explainer channels tell owners to skip locators, while David Church works business lists as a locator, targeting 15 to 20 corporations to land two or three.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator working business-name recoveries starts from the same premise: this is earned revenue that slipped through operational cracks, not windfall cash. GardenShop.Pro's Tennessee breakdown frames it as uncashed vendor checks, returned electronic transfers, unreturned security deposits and forgotten insurance claims that land with the state after an office move or personnel change, with vendor payments sitting one to three years and government or municipal credits escheating after a single year [bUxdjo_bs0g @ 00:01:02]. Как се прави's North Dakota run puts hard dormancy clocks on the most common business assets: mineral proceeds and royalties at three years, vendor payments and credit memos at two, utility refunds at one, which means a missed final utility deposit after a relocation hits the state twelve months later [7MUtjq4bwU0 @ 00:01:48]. The custody model is equally consistent across states. South Carolina holds escheated assets in perpetual custody with zero statute of limitations, so funds turned over twenty years ago are as claimable as funds turned over two years ago [KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:01:37], and Colorado runs the identical no-expiration rule, with a five-year general dormancy and just one year for unclaimed payroll [2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:01:21]. The operator read is simple: the clock never runs out on the owner, so old entities, acquired subsidiaries and decade-old addresses are all live inventory worth sweeping.

The second point of full agreement: the state search itself costs nothing, but a single portal never covers the whole map. GardenShop.Pro's Missouri walkthrough is blunt that the treasurer never, ever charges a fee to search, claim or return property [fntI1mKZpK0 @ 00:04:04]. Как се прави's Virginia session pushes past the state line, pairing vamoneysearch.gov with missingmoney.com because an out-of-state incorporation or a national vendor base routinely parks money in other jurisdictions [RtDPQUDYTy0 @ 00:03:47]. Garden Shop Pro's corporation-name guide adds the jurisdictional split that catches most teams: federal agencies are exempt from state escheatment, so IRS refunds, bankruptcy-court distributions, closed-bank FDIC deposits and matured savings bonds will never show on missingmoney.com and need a separate federal track, starting with IRS Form 3911 for an undelivered corporate refund [7Fc0D2RuIJE @ 00:03:14]. Even inside one state the online index leaks. Rhode Island's findrimoney.gov only displays properties valued above one dollar, so micro-balances and certain restricted asset classes require a direct call to the Unclaimed Property Division at 401-462-7676, while bankruptcy dividends sit in the separate U.S. Bankruptcy Unclaimed Funds Locator for the District of Rhode Island [an41g6w5nlU @ 00:03:11]. Operators therefore treat state, multi-state, federal and phone-only channels as four distinct sweeps rather than one search.

Proof is the third consensus pillar, and every speaker stresses that business claims face a heavier burden than individual ones. Как се прави's Minnesota guide lays out a four-part package: federal tax ID verification through a W-9 or CP575, a letter of authorization on company letterhead signed by an officer such as the CEO or CFO, proof tying the business to the old address on the record through bank statements, leases or vendor contracts, and a government photo ID for the signer [NPH35-KUMjQ @ 00:04:20]. GardenShop.Pro's Connecticut breakdown names the same three tests, legal identity, corporate authority and asset nexus, and insists the nexus document show the business operated at the exact address tied to the funds [mTurQziolOk @ 00:03:02]. Georgia's version layers on a current Secretary of State annual registration to prove active status, calling the historical address record the main defense against corporate identity theft [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:04:09]. Structural history changes the stack. Under Delaware section 278, former officers can claim freely inside a three-year post-dissolution survival window; after that, section 279 requires a Court of Chancery petition to appoint a receiver, though the Kraft Murphy ruling held that residual assets still legally belong to the company [7Fc0D2RuIJE @ 00:04:16].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Execution starts with the field trap that multiple Как се прави walkthroughs flag as the number-one reason business searches come back empty. On North Dakota's unclaimedproperty.nd.gov, the company name goes in the last-name field and the first-name field stays completely blank; typing even a space or an initial forces the algorithm to filter out commercial entities, returning zero matches while the state holds thousands of dollars [7MUtjq4bwU0 @ 00:02:53]. Once the field is right, the variant stack does the heavy lifting. The Minnesota guide has operators search DBAs, common misspellings, versions without Inc. or LLC, former names of absorbed predecessors, and every name containing an ampersand or hyphen both with and without the punctuation, repeating the sweep a couple of times a year as new property lands [NPH35-KUMjQ @ 00:03:36]. Colorado's breakdown explains why this matters: financial institutions truncate long names and drop designators before remitting, so Acme Manufacturing Incorporated must also be run as Acme, Acme MFG and Acme Manufacturing [2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:03:25]. GardenShop.Pro's Missouri tip closes the loop by stripping leading articles, searching Smith Corporation instead of The Smith Corporation, on the business tab of showmemoney.com [fntI1mKZpK0 @ 00:03:17]. City, zip code and state-issued property ID filters then narrow bloated result pools down to the branches that actually match.

The filing mechanics are technical, and rejections come from format errors as often as from missing proof. Colorado's portal requires the unique numeric claim ID generated at initiation, accepts only PDF, TIFF, PNG or JPEG, caps each file at exactly 10 megabytes, refuses password-protected or encrypted files, and takes five documents per upload session, so a large merger packet goes up in sequential batches under that same claim ID [2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:04:44]. Minnesota adds file names under 100 characters using only letters, numbers, dashes or underscores, while original stock certificates and safe deposit box contents still have to be mailed physically [NPH35-KUMjQ @ 00:05:34]. Payout rules vary just as sharply. Georgia quotes roughly 30 to 90 days of standard processing once documents are uploaded or mailed, and pays approved monetary claims exclusively by physical paper check to the registered address, with direct deposit and electronic transfers strictly prohibited [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:04:39]. That check carries its own trap: South Carolina refund checks void 90 days from the date of issue, which bounces the funds back into the central database and forces a full re-filing of the manual claim form and every verification document from scratch, so treasury teams are told to cash the disbursement immediately on receipt [KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:05:27].

David Church of Surplus Institute works the same databases from the opposite chair, as a locator chasing business balances for a fee. His workflow: get registered in a locator-friendly state, download its unclaimed list, drop the spreadsheet into a paid ChatGPT account and prompt it to separate the highest-paid business claims, for example the top 40 [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:09:41]. He then has AI trace corporate ownership and goes after someone in the accounting department or the president with a plain pitch: hey, I found some unclaimed property, you have quite a bit, I do this, I would love to work with you, sometimes sent as a letter. His math is pure volume: line up 15 to 20 corporations, local banks included, and expect to collect on two or three [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:15:44]. State fee rules bound that model. Missouri voids any locator agreement signed in the first 12 months of state custody, then caps fees at 10% in year two, 15% in year three and 20% after 36 months [fntI1mKZpK0 @ 00:05:23]. Georgia goes further at the search stage itself, forcing users to electronically certify a valid legal or equitable interest under OCGA 44-12-215, which restricts speculative third-party queries aimed at corporate records [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:03:19].

callout.title: Search Hacks That Surface Hidden Business Balances
callout.body: Operators who only type the current legal name into one state portal leave money behind. These four moves pull up records that standard searches miss.
items: Search Tennessee's claimittn.gov by FEIN rather than name where possible; the federal employer identification number is called an even better match key than the precise business name [GardenShop.Pro — bUxdjo_bs0g @ 00:02:18]

Run the zip codes of every former office location; if a vendor misspelled the company name on a refund check 10 years ago, that old zip code may be the only way to spot it [GardenShop.Pro — rOaTjN9BoFE @ 00:04:31]

In South Carolina hit three portals, not one: the primary database, the outstanding state-issued checks database for uncashed government checks over two years old, and the SC Vendor Electronic Payment Search by federal EIN for missing ACH deposits [Как се прави — KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:03:10]

In Oklahoma add the Oklahoma City municipal database for uncashed city checks and contractor deposits, plus the state's online archive of bi-annual newspaper unclaimed property supplements [Как се прави — M3F5IgHI7Ow @ 00:05:06]

sop_steps.action: List the legal name, every DBA, truncations, suffix-free versions, acquired entities, punctuation variants and former zip codes.
sop_steps.detail: Search with and without Inc., LLC or Corp., include dissolved subsidiaries and acquired units, and remember funds escheated right before a merger stay listed under the original entity name on file at the time [Как се прави — KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:03:56]

sop_steps.title: Run Every Portal Correctly
sop_steps.action: Search each state portal using only the last or business name field, then missingmoney.com and the federal locators.
sop_steps.detail: On Oklahoma's yourmoney.ok.gov the full legal business name goes in the last-name box with the first-name box empty; start broad and add city or zip only when results are unmanageable [Как се прави — M3F5IgHI7Ow @ 00:03:04]

sop_steps.title: Assemble the Evidence Package
sop_steps.action: Gather FEIN proof, officer authority, signer photo ID, historical address nexus and any succession documents before filing.
sop_steps.detail: Virginia's baseline is a signed claim form, a W-9 or FEIN assignment letter, the signing officer's photo ID and proof linking the business to the historical address such as an old lease, tax filing or utility invoice, plus merger, dissolution or assumed name records where structure changed [Как се прави — RtDPQUDYTy0 @ 00:05:12]

sop_steps.action: Upload under the numeric claim ID, track auditing status online, and deposit the state check the day it arrives.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who gets paid. David Church of Surplus Institute runs locating as a commission business and defends it hard. They booked a 74,000 commission on a Florida client who knew about 300,000, then surfaced another 250,000 in a deep dive, and they say their students and they have claimed over 71 million [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:02:19]. Church points to Utah's fee finder rule allowing 20% and pushes operators to register in locator-friendly states, while calling out Virginia and West Virginia staff who told them no locator should earn a fee on money the state collects interest on [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:07:42]. The explainer channels pull the opposite way. GardenShop.Pro's Missouri breakdown cites Haven Savings Bank v. Zanellini, where a 35% contingency put an owner on the hook for over $53,000 on a roughly $164,000 recovery. They say Missouri voids any agreement in the first 12 months, then caps fees at 10%, 15%, and 20% after 36 months [fntI1mKZpK0 @ 00:04:49]. Garden Shop Pro's corporate guide says flatly not to give a third away to a middleman [7Fc0D2RuIJE @ 00:05:51]. Georgia splits the difference. General agents max out at 10%, but registered claimant's designated representatives who pay a $1,200 annual fee may charge up to 30% [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:07:12].

Practitioners also split on how to fire the first query. One camp starts tight. Как се прави's North Dakota walkthrough says the engine uses exact string matching first, so operators should run the full legal name including LLC or Incorporated, then a truncated root like Acme, then Acme Ind, then vendor misspellings, former trade names, and acquired entities [7MUtjq4bwU0 @ 00:05:58]. The other camp strips names down from the start. Как се прави's Virginia company guide tells searchers to drop LLC, Inc., or Corp. on the first pass to cast a better net. Next they hit trade names and DBAs, because holders generate property records from what was printed on an everyday invoice, not the formal corporate charter name [RtDPQUDYTy0 @ 00:03:17]. Georgia's version goes further. When the initial search comes up empty, searchers flip the less specific match toggle to catch typographical errors, truncated business names, and missing suffixes the reporting company typed wrong years ago, then refine by county or municipal zip code [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:02:51]. GardenShop.Pro's Missouri guide adds a smaller wrinkle the others skip: omit leading articles, so the query reads Smith Corporation rather than The Smith Corporation [fntI1mKZpK0 @ 00:03:17]. In practice the stripped-down and exact passes end up run back to back, because each catches records the other misses.

Cadence and scale are the third fault line. The corporate-explainer camp treats searching as internal hygiene on a timer. Как се прави's Rhode Island guide wants bi-annual searches in Q1 and Q3, with every DBA, typo, and legacy name re-run each time. It also calls for a phone call to the Unclaimed Property Division for micro balances the website will not display [an41g6w5nlU @ 00:06:12]. David Church plays a different game entirely. Instead of sweeping one company's names, they register in a state, download its spreadsheet, and drop it into ChatGPT to pull the top 20 or 40 business claims. Then they hunt owners through corporate filings, investor relations, and accounting departments [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:17:11]. Their math is volume rather than certainty. They contact 15 to 20 corporations, accept that a Texas Instruments probably will not sign, and expect to collect on two or three of the batch [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:15:44]. They also skip the small stuff, saying a claim worth 200 is not worth working when bigger payouts are on the board. David Daniels of HBU Asset Recovery pitches the plainest frame of the group. Search each state where the owner lived or worked, file a claim with proof of identity, and wait for the office to verify before the assets come back [Zq6923LSEX4 @ 00:00:31].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common self-inflicted miss is the first name box. Как се прави's North Dakota walkthrough warns that typing even a space or an initial there makes the search algorithm filter out commercial entities entirely. The result is zero matches even when the state is holding thousands for the company [7MUtjq4bwU0 @ 00:02:53]. The Minnesota guide calls it the absolute wrong way to search, because it forces the database to treat the query like a human being's name [NPH35-KUMjQ @ 00:03:06]. The Oklahoma guide says that if operators take away one thing, it should be that the entire legal business name goes in the last name field with the first name left empty [M3F5IgHI7Ow @ 00:02:51]. The second trap is trusting one database to hold everything. Garden Shop Pro's corporate guide stresses that federal agencies are exempt from state escheatment, so money owed by the IRS or a federal bankruptcy court will never appear on the multi-state portal [7Fc0D2RuIJE @ 00:03:14]. That side runs on separate tools: IRS Form 3911 for an undelivered corporate tax refund, the bankruptcy courts' unclaimed funds locator for a debtor that went under, FDIC checks for deposits from closed banks, and a separate lookup for matured corporate savings bonds. Skip that track and the federal checks never surface at all.

Paperwork is where found money stalls. Как се прави's Colorado walkthrough says a standard cash claim under $5,000 needs an online form, a W-9, a photo ID, and proof of authority, and takes 90 to 150 days. Merged or dissolved entities need certified articles, a certificate of good standing, and a 6 to 12-month audit of the ownership chain [2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:03:58]. Their upload rules punish sloppiness: PDF, TIFF, PNG, or JPEG only, 10 megabytes per file, and five documents per session. Any password or encryption gets the file rejected. Georgia's guide shows the acquisition trap with a forgotten $10,000 utility deposit sitting under a dissolved target. The buyer cannot claim it with its current FEIN. It takes FEINs for both the target and the surviving entity, plus the certificate of merger [WHTvjELqLw0 @ 00:05:23]. Garden Shop Pro flags the Delaware clock. After the 3-year survival window under section 278 closes, a dissolved corporation needs a Court of Chancery receiver under section 279 to sign for and collect the funds [7Fc0D2RuIJE @ 00:04:16]. GardenShop.Pro's Tennessee guide adds that payouts for dissolved companies split by historical equity. A 60% owner collects 60% only if the operating agreements and stock ledgers survived [bUxdjo_bs0g @ 00:03:32].

Even approved claims die on the back end. Как се прави's South Carolina guide warns that state refund checks carry a strict 90-day validity window. Miss it and the check voids, the funds bounce back into the central database, and the team must refile the entire manual claim and verification package from scratch [KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:05:27]. GardenShop.Pro's Connecticut breakdown gives automated CT Big Match warrants for single-owner property under $2,500 just 180 days before they go void [mTurQziolOk @ 00:03:59]. On the locator side, David Church reports the economics are lumpy and leaky. Owners go around the locator once they learn the money exists, like a buyer who shops at one dealer and signs at another. One Florida woman sitting on 108,000 called the police on the letters until a detective confirmed the funds, and she collected with no locator in the middle [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:01:35]. Their own client had already been denied on part of a claim that never should have been denied. Their prospecting stack also breaks. ChatGPT cut them off for searching too much, YouTube pulled a business spreadsheet as personal information and they lost the appeal, and a live Sun Holdings lookup turned up only small amounts not worth chasing [EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:20:12].

callout.title: Four checks before a business-name claim goes out the door
callout.body: Every one of these stalls came straight from practitioners who watched claims die, checks void, or contracts get voided. Clear all four before filing or pitching.
items: Confirm the state's locator timing window and fee cap before pitching: Missouri voids deals in the first 12 months and Colorado in the first 24 months, with Colorado capping fees at 10% [Как се прави — 2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:07:20].
Assemble the full ownership chain before filing on any merged or dissolved entity, because those claims run a 6 to 12-month audit of the legal lineage [Как се прави — 2_XKdBsmJ5c @ 00:04:15].
Calendar the payout window the day the check is printed: South Carolina checks void at 90 days and force a full refile from scratch [Как се прави — KJU4iu_xIgw @ 00:05:43].

Price the pipeline on volume, not single deals: contact 15 to 20 corporations to collect on two or three, and skip small claims not worth the work [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — EFuzXe23Q7I @ 00:16:00].

chapters.question_prompt: What investigator requirements, contract changes, and filing procedures must an operator understand before assisting with state claims?
chapters.title: Investigator Requirements and State Claim Filing
chapters.subtitle: California registration and contracts, Texas private-investigator discussions, skip-tracing license warnings, powers of attorney, notarized Pennsylvania and Utah forms, and state claim walkthroughs
chapters.executive_summary: Licensed recovery operators agree on two gates before any state claim pays: a fee ceiling and a license or registration. Texas investigators Sharalyn Criswell and Michelle, along with David Church working California's investigator agreement, all operate under a 10% cap. ShadowAnyone's Larry Kay warns that charging above a state's cap can count as unlicensed investigative work and bar a PI license for life. California registration is an emailed packet that is usually approved within days. Texas requires a DPS background check, fingerprinting, and PI sponsorship at $295 per year, or three years of experience plus an in-person exam to run an agency. The street mechanics are clean agreements, ID, SSN and address proof, self-built checklists, and tracked shipping. Church reports checks of $1,400 to $1,600 on mid-size claims. Operators split on workarounds: some push direct family deals and pre-escheat agreements, while Michelle relies on volume instead.

key_metrics.label: Texas Licensed PI Fee Cap
key_metrics.value: 10% of the claim amount
key_metrics.context: Sharalyn Criswell states the Texas Comptroller by law restricts a licensed private investigator from taking more than 10% for assisting a claimant, with the state paying the claimant directly.

key_metrics.label: Texas PI Sponsorship Fee
key_metrics.value: $295 per year, renewed annually
key_metrics.context: Michelle sponsors registrants under their agency one year at a time, which gives them a usable license number. This bypasses the three years of experience needed for an operator's own license.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The 10% ceiling is the first number every licensed operator in this lane quotes. Sharalyn Criswell, a Texas licensed private investigator, states that the Texas Comptroller by law restricts a licensed PI from taking more than 10% for assisting a claimant. Criswell adds that under the assisted-claim process the investigator never touches the money, because the state sends it straight to the claimant [yiH-ZfQj-oc @ 00:04:31]. Money Making Juggernaut host Eric confirms the same Texas structure: you must be a registered PI or be sponsored by a PI company, and you are capped at 10% [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:02:15]. On the California side, David Church of Surplus Institute walks through the standard investigator agreement. Church reads the clause assigning the investigator a percentage not to exceed 10% of the net assets the claimant recovers, payable upon payment of the claim, and calls the state cut and dry on that point [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:03:46]. Larry Kay of ShadowAnyone calls the cap the missing link that get-rich unclaimed funds courses never teach. Kay says one state they know caps finder's fees at ten percent, and that charging more than a state allows means you are committing a crime [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:05:32]. The operating baseline is simple: price every state unclaimed funds deal at or under the statutory ceiling before the first outreach call goes out, and build the business around that number.

Licensing or registration is the second non-negotiable. Michelle, a Texas PI licensed for four years who also runs an agency, says the licensing requirement has been debated. However, the state's own FAQ says plainly you must be licensed, and even requesting the monthly list requires a company name and a license number [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:04:45]. Kay warns that the downside of getting this wrong goes well past a lawsuit. Some states bar anyone with an infraction or conviction for unlicensed investigative work from ever getting a PI license, and in the places Kay knows, that ban has no time limit [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:06:30]. California sits at the opposite end of the friction scale. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO calls California the most investigator-friendly state in the nation. Green points to a dedicated investigator unit and an official investigator handbook, and says calls and emails are answered close to same day, with walk-in help available at the office [3_qKwnM5EUw @ 00:00:17]. Eric adds that you can become a registered finder in California simply by emailing paperwork, and in Massachusetts by filling out a one-pager. Eric says that registration, posted on your website, immediately establishes more credibility with skeptical claimants [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:07:05]. Every operator treats the license or registration number as both the legal entry ticket and a front-line trust signal that shortens the sales conversation with claimants and their families.

Across every state operators demonstrate, the filing packet rests on the same three proofs. FOX6 reporter Jenna Sacks says Wisconsin asks for proof of identity, a Social Security number, and proof of address. Sacks adds that if a claimant lacks one of those items, they should submit what they have, because it may be enough [Cb8M7-NxR50 @ 00:02:57]. Unclaimed CEO tells investigators to read California's filing instructions in detail because the claimant's Social Security number will be needed. When the reporting company never supplied a social, the state asks for additional documentation instead [2SYC3A6apHk @ 00:03:08]. The Utah explainer quotes a former unclaimed property worker who says address matching is the primary requirement. The worker explains that any John Smith could try to claim cash reported at a given address, so historic utility bills, old tax returns, or past driver's licenses matching that exact address are the claimant's golden ticket [edHsQGppnKE @ 00:05:30]. On the consumer side of the same pipeline, The Accidental Publisher shows the Texas flow. The claimant picks their claimant type, confirms the mailing address and email, receives a claim ID with a document upload link, and then waits 60 to 90 days for the money [ODgVh05VyTg @ 00:01:55]. An investigator's job is to deliver a packet that clears identity, social, and address verification on the first pass.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: California registration runs off page 12 of the investigator handbook. Joe Green says the packet must list the investigator plus everyone who will call and follow up on claims, including a virtual assistant, spouse, or child. The packet includes copies of driver's licenses and Social Security numbers so the state knows each person is real, and Green notes that a stateside VA counts [3_qKwnM5EUw @ 00:02:04]. Green builds a one-page template listing name and attachments such as a driver's license, veteran's ID card, and social, plus a real phone number, business address, and email. Green warns against fake addresses like 123 Party Lane because the unit has to call you. Approval usually arrives by email within a few days [3_qKwnM5EUw @ 00:03:32]. Texas is heavier. Michelle demonstrates the DPS portal step by step. You start an individual application, choose unarmed registration, select private investigator, enter the sponsoring business's ID, and keep the job duties brief by listing skip tracing and locating heirs. Michelle says that wording also smooths approvals with skip tracing vendors like TLO and IDI Core [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:10:29]. Sponsored registrants need a background check and fingerprinting but no exam. Running your own agency takes three years of experience plus an in-person exam, which is why Michelle sponsors registrants one year at a time for $295, renewed annually [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:12:09].

David Church fills out California's standard investigator agreement line by line. When working with an heir, the heir's name goes in the claimant slot and the investigator's name below it, never the deceased's. The deceased owner's name and reported address still go in the property block exactly as reported, along with the holder such as Wells Fargo, the account type, the amount, and the property ID [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:02:03]. Church draws an arrow and an asterisk at every initial spot, writes 10 as the agreed percentage, and notes the agreement now runs 12 months instead of six [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:06:55]. For line items worth a few cents, Church simply tells the claimant they exist rather than papering them; one file carried 50 claims. When a claimant balks at writing their social on the form, Church sends a self-addressed stamped envelope so the claimant mails it to the state directly, or has them disclose it by email to the state. Unclaimed CEO converts the state's filing instructions into a Google Doc checklist, signs off on it, and includes it in the filing as a cover sheet. Their reasoning is that with state verification, more is more [2SYC3A6apHk @ 00:05:21]. Eric runs a Zoom screen share with signed clients through the entire online form, which makes collecting the social easier. Michelle accepts that approach or a prefilled PDF the client returns [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:30:33].

Under the cap, the economics are a volume game. Church says 10% of claims in the $14,000 to $16,000 range produces $1,400 to $1,600 checks, and landing a couple of those a week means you are doing nicely [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:18]. Larry Kay runs the counter-math. 10% of a $10,000 fund is $1,000 and worth the effort. However, 10% of a $280 fund is $28, which will not cover a paid database lookup or courthouse parking and time [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:04:00]. Michelle says Texas holds over 100,000 claims in a list that is updated monthly but so large that almost nobody can open it. Operators either build a database, have one built, or buy counties from group member Shannon Price. Licensed operators get the Texas update free by emailing the state by the 7th of each month, while other states charge; Massachusetts required a money order [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:29:14]. Michelle says that at roughly $2,000 per deal, telemarketers, VAs, and mailers can stay busy forever, and that the volume more than makes up for the low percentage. Eric scripts outreach from the list data itself. The script references the holder and report year, such as Chase reporting funds in 2002, asks whether this is the correct John Smith, and follows up with screenshots in an intro email [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:31:53]. Michelle reports Texas collections landing in 45 days at the fastest and up to six months.

callout.body: Small moves on disclosure, cost separation, timing, and shipping protect the fee when the percentage itself cannot move.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Licensing is the first fork, and the operators split hard on how heavy the entry ticket should be. Michelle, the licensed Texas PI on the Money Making Juggernaut call, admits the statute has been debated, but the Texas FAQ says plainly you must be licensed, and Michelle would rather practice legally than gamble on the ambiguity [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:04:45]. That route means a background check, fingerprinting, agency sponsorship, and a three-year experience wall before running your own agency, with a three-to-four-hour in-person exam on the far side. California sits at the opposite pole. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO calls it the most investigator-friendly state in the nation: mail or email a simple template with driver's license and Social Security proof, use real phone numbers and addresses, and approval usually arrives by email within a few days [3_qKwnM5EUw @ 00:03:32]. Eric, hosting the Juggernaut call, stacks those easy registrations with the Massachusetts one-pager and puts the numbers on the website for credibility. Larry Kay of ShadowAnyone frames the downside: skip the homework and some states treat your finder work as unlicensed investigative services, an infraction that bans you from a PI license for life with no time limit [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:06:47]. Pennsylvania adds a wrinkle raised on the same call: finders must be licensed there, but attorneys are exempt [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:20:20].

The fee cap is where the playbooks really diverge. Sharalyn Criswell of Texas Licensed Private Investigator treats the 10% comptroller cap as an honor-system ceiling, pitching businesses with a handshake and a small contract, and stressing that the state sends the check straight to the claimant so the investigator never touches the money [yiH-ZfQj-oc @ 00:04:31]. David Church of Surplus Institute reads the 2023 California standard investigator agreement the same way: a percentage not to exceed 10% of net assets recovered, so David writes ten by default and only drops lower on a huge amount [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:03]. Larry Kay starts from the economics, saying an operator might decide 30% is the fair price for the work, then warns that if your state caps finder fees, charging over that line means you are committing a crime [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:05:32]. Eric pushes the grey zone: a client signed before funds get sheeted to the state still receives the check and pays the invoice under the existing agreement, and a family member you help privately can pay you directly, so Eric tells listeners not to let the cap stop them from charging the percentage they want [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:27:00]. Michelle declines to test any workaround and says volume more than makes up for the percentage.

Filing tactics split along security, speed, and paperwork style. Joe Green builds rapport to get Social Security numbers without hesitation, then converts the state's filing instructions into a Google Doc checklist that rides in the package as a signed cover sheet, on the logic that with the state more is more [2SYC3A6apHk @ 00:05:05]. David Church takes a different route on the SSN: when a claimant balks, send a self-addressed stamped envelope so the claimant mails the number to the state directly, or forward the state's email and let the claimant disclose it there [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:07:39]. Eric hops on a Zoom screen-share with every signed client, searching the name and filling the form together, because the sensitive Social Security step goes easier live; Michelle offers the alternative of building your own app, collecting the data, and sending it over as a PDF [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:30:33]. On shipping, Joe Green overnights and tracks every package because the goal is getting paid, while conceding regular mail gets there when it gets there. The yellow-paper rule is contested too: Joe Green points to the handbook's yellow cover sheet guidance, but David Church reports getting paid on notarized forms that never touched yellow paper [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:09:47].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is credibility. Sharalyn Criswell approached businesses holding comptroller money and got treated like the fraud, with skeptics refusing to believe a state-licensed PI was real, and Sharalyn concedes the approach probably could have been different [yiH-ZfQj-oc @ 00:01:46]. Worse, one business with roughly $30,000 sitting at the comptroller ran the tip past its company attorney, then cut Sharalyn out entirely, even though the company only learned the money existed because of that outreach [yiH-ZfQj-oc @ 00:04:10]. Sharalyn's adjustment was holding back the full dollar amount early and leading with the legitimacy of the comptroller source. David Church flags the opposite disclosure trap on the California agreement: clause three says that if the investigator fails to disclose the nature and value of the property before signing, and the claimant believes it would have been recovered anyway, the claimant owes nothing [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:51]. David's read is that finders are filling in amounts afterward and hiding the real figure, and David would rather take $2,500 on a $50,000 claim than get nothing [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:05:55]. Clause four adds a cost trap: if the claim fails, notary fees, FedEx, and every other out-of-pocket expense stay on the investigator, with no recourse against the client.

Unit economics kill more finder operations than regulators do. Larry Kay runs the math on a $280 claim at a 10% cap: $28, which does not cover a paid database lookup, courthouse parking, or your time [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:04:00]. Larry adds that the $3,700, $5,000, and $10,000 claims are getting harder to find because more people are working them and owners can search online themselves [5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:02:44]. David Church shows the other side of the ledger, regularly cashing $1,400 to $1,600 checks and noting a couple of those a week means you are doing nicely [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:18]. David also refuses to chase dust: when an owner has a pile of three-cent and 25-cent accounts, David just tells the claimant they exist rather than paperworking fifty claims. Michelle's answer to the cap is raw volume: Texas emails licensed PIs a free updated statewide list by the seventh of each month, and an operator happy to make $2,000 a deal could stay busy forever with telemarketers, VAs, and mailers [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:29:31]. The catch is the file is so large hardly anyone can open it, so you either build your own database or buy county cuts from Shannon Price.

Time and death are the slowest killers. David Church describes a $1,500 California probate claim where the state kept surfacing last-minute document demands, stretching start to payout to roughly eight months, which David calls ludicrous [D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:07:11]. That is why the agreement's validity jumping from six to twelve months matters. Michelle reports Texas payouts as fast as 45 days but stretching up to six months, and Eric warns that stocks, bonds, and mutual funds get confusing because the cash is sometimes not pulled yet [vp2uuB23fww @ 00:29:52]. Deceased owners are the hard wall: the GardenShop.Pro explainer warns that a power of attorney dies with the principal, and anyone using a voided POA on a dead relative's property faces claim rejection plus civil liability and fiduciary misconduct accusations [dhZB_jSn2Qg @ 00:06:17]. Waiting can erase the money outright. FOX6 reports that a Milwaukee man's mother had $12,582 listed in a 2002 newspaper ad; by the time Jerry tried to claim it, the escheated estate had passed its 10-year hold and lapsed to the Wisconsin common school fund [Cb8M7-NxR50 @ 00:01:17]. List access is its own bottleneck: Eric sent Georgia a money order and still has no list.

callout.title: Kill Switches Before You Sign a Claimant
callout.body: Every one of these stops cost a working operator money, a license, or a payout. Clear all four before the agreement goes out.
items: Confirm your license or registration status in the target state before outreach, because unlicensed investigative work can bar you from a PI license with no time limit [ShadowAnyone — 5gSBjAC1g0s @ 00:06:09].

Write the agreed percentage at or under 10% on California and Texas agreements and mark every spot the claimant must initial [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:18].

Disclose the nature and value of the property before execution, or clause three lets the claimant walk away owing nothing [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — D3Fcqm3xaco @ 00:04:51].
If the reported owner is deceased, stop any power of attorney use and route the claim through a court-appointed personal representative [GardenShop.Pro — dhZB_jSn2Qg @ 00:06:01].

chapters.question_prompt: How do practitioners locate claimants, investigate deceased owners, and work with heirs and estate representatives?
chapters.title: Skip Tracing, Heirs, and Estate Claims
chapters.subtitle: Free tracing websites, Skipmatrix and other tracing software, common tracing mistakes, deceased-owner research, heir claims, Mississippi procedures, and Ohio estate-attorney guidance
chapters.executive_summary: Skip tracing heirs and estate claims is a family-reconstruction business. Tamara, the Ohio Division of Unclaimed Funds and David Church agree the money sits with states in perpetuity and that deceased owners, some dead 40 to 50 years, hold much of it. Sean Boujie, Joe Green and Church agree relatives and associates are the fastest route to a claimant, with Boujie reporting a 40 to 50% hit-rate lift. The street stack runs on paid data: Tracers at $1 to $1.50 per skip, Skip Matrix at $0.14 per hit, Skipify at 15 cents per record, and batch lead stacker at about $40 a month. All of them beat free sites, which run at 40 to 60% accuracy. Fees split the field: Church asked 50% on a hard $14,000 deceased file, while Ohio caps finders at 10% and Tamara tells prospects they can file on their own.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Tamara is a licensed private investigator who works tax-foreclosure surplus and state unclaimed property. She describes every state treasury as a lost-and-found that holds money into perpetuity. The Ohio Division of Unclaimed Funds runs on the same terms: roughly $4B held, $109.5M returned last year, and accrued interest paid to the claimant [YoID4SzRBaI @ 00:01:01] [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:07:03]. The first rule both sides repeat is to stop searching only living names. Tamara tells families to run every deceased relative, because some assets have sat untouched for decades. Ohio outreach administrator Susie Wagner says most of the state's $4B belongs to people over 50, and she points to State Fair finds such as a $50,000 insurance heir and $71,000 in forgotten dividends [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:28:13]. That turns a database lookup into a genealogy job. Tamara works files where the owner has been dead 40 to 50 years. Those files require a complete family tree plus a death certificate for every intermediate heir in the chain [YoID4SzRBaI @ 00:05:40]. The treasury calls registered locators heir finders and gives them a database of millions of names. Tamara uses the forms and treasury contacts she already has to speed up payouts. Finding the money is not the hard part. The operator's edge is rebuilding the family that can legally collect it.

Every skip tracer here agrees the claimant is rarely the easiest person to reach. Sean Boujie calls skip tracing a separate skill set, because foreclosed owners end up living in cars, in basements, or on a friend's couch. He uses MicroBilt for its strength in finding relatives and associates. He then mails letters to those relatives under the ex-owner's name and leaves messages for them, because there is always an aunt. The higher upfront spend lifts his hit rate 40 to 50% [ujbTh1In_c4 @ 00:02:37]. Joe of Unclaimed CEO names ignoring the possible relatives shown on TruePeopleSearch as the first of his three biggest skip tracing mistakes. Relatives vouch for you, and that is what produces callbacks [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:02:39]. David Church runs the same play on deceased files. He starts with the newest-dated mobile numbers, because kids keep their deceased parents' phones. He then works the 'R' relatives flag, because a claimant who cannot be found means the funds escheat [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:00:39]. Eric of Money Making Juggernaut closed a California deal this way, through the owner's son, who held power of attorney [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:13:35]. Across every one of these operators, the family is the way in, and the person on the file is often the last one reached.

The third point of agreement is that free data holds back a serious operation. Joe Green puts free people-search sites at 50 to 60% accuracy, with updates only two or three times a year. BeenVerified runs 70 to 80% and refreshes every two to three months [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:02:37]. David Wilkerson, who came over from off-market real estate, rates free sites even lower, at 40 to 50%, and uses them only for single manual skips. Once deals start landing, he says you have to pay for data and move into bulk cold calls and voice drops [Tx1_986LmrY @ 00:01:57]. Shai Korn of Skip Matrix sums up the argument in one line: your tools are everything [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:52:24]. On the claim side, the baseline prerequisite is paperwork. Ohio division counsel Kelly Lister and Wagner require an unexpired ID, proof of address from a utility or government agency, a W-2 or 1099 as SSN proof, and a W-9 on every claim. Decedent claims under $3,000 cumulative go through an expedited path: an unredacted death certificate, marriage or birth certificates, and a table of heirship. Claims of $3,000 or more need a probate order dated within two years, a reopened estate for a newly discovered asset, and the estate TIN [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:42:53].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The phone setup comes first. Joe Green never dials from a personal cell. He runs Nurture Ninja on Twilio, where numbers cost about $1 against a $10 minimum balance that auto-recharges. He buys local area codes, because a Missouri number calling Florida gets ignored [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:01:06]. For data, he prices Tracers at $100 to $200 a month in packages, or roughly $10 setup plus $1.50 per skip. He calls that cost trivial once ten deals return $10,000 to $20,000. Joe of Unclaimed CEO prices Tracers closer to $1 per skip and says it pulls daily from 6,000 sources. By comparison, TruePeopleSearch refreshes about quarterly, and BeenVerified costs about $29 [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:04:30]. Wilkerson's bulk pick, which he calls batch lead stacker, runs about $40 a month plus 15 cents a skip. It charges nothing for no-hit files, filters duplicates across lists, and includes a free litigation scrub. His rule is that paying 15 cents a file is worth it all day long if accuracy climbs 30 or 40% [xqXetexqH30 @ 00:03:05]. Skipify offers 15 cents per record pay-as-you-go, or $99 a month for 750 skips, which works out to about 13 cents each. Unused skips carry over and never expire [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:06:54].

Skip Matrix COO Shai Korn starts from the premise that raw county data is broken. He sees APNs where addresses should be, county and state APNs mixed up, and full names jammed into one column. His fix is a waterfall. It formats the data, updates mailing addresses through USPS NCOA, and then runs three-step skip tracing. The output includes deceased, vacancy and bankruptcy flags, five relatives and five associates with relationship labels, about 120 contacts per lead, and 480 columns [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:11:20]. Pricing tops out at $0.14 per hit, paid upfront with misses refunded. There is a 100-record minimum, or a flat $15 for smaller batches ($14 with the code Surplus). Turnaround is usually under an hour [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:17:09]. Eric still moved his volume to Skipify for two reasons: a built-in DNC check and no minimum order [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:15:27]. His sharpest file rule concerns address-only lookups, which return the current owner. They are only reliable on sales less than two months old. For anything older, upload the prior owner's name together with the address, and have VAs at $5 an hour prepare the file [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:29:21]. When results come back, phones 1 through 5 are ranked by how often sources saw them, so check the last-seen dates before dialing.

Outreach is scripted and uses repeated touches across channels. David Church opens calls with his own name and the name of the person he is trying to reach, then cites the property address and account. His emails put the details in an attached PDF or Google Doc, which he says avoids spam filters. They use a businesslike subject line and state that the message is not a solicitation or sales call [2l827py8Fe8 @ 00:00:55]. On deceased files, he runs Google Advanced Search on the name, the city and the word obituary with a date filter, and he searches ancestry.com and legacy.com. He also calls convalescent homes and memorial or funeral centers with a script, repeats those calls three or four times, and will work as many as 22 associates on one file [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:05:14]. Joe Green combines official-looking letters with what he calls monster follow-up on social media: friend the target's family members first, then DM the target [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:05:51]. Joe of Unclaimed CEO caps his pipeline at five to ten people a week, tops, and works each one for 14 to 21 days. He will chase a $7,000-profit lead for two to four weeks, because the data always drives his decision [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:07:48]. Eric's Tennessee claim took five touches before it landed.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among operators is the fee itself. David Church of Surplus Institute works a hard deceased-owner file with roughly $14,000 in surplus and says they would ask 50%, because summary administration and probate work pile onto the job, with their attorney taking about $1,500 plus 5% [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:01:31]. On a separate heir case, Church quotes a flat 10% with the pitch that the client pays nothing otherwise, though the numbers they give do not reconcile: the claim is called $516,000 while the 10% cut landed at $1,500, and they also filed a free $60 side claim for the same client [2l827py8Fe8 @ 00:03:36]. The regulator view runs the other direction. Ohio Division Counsel Kelly Lister says finder compensation is capped at 10%, stays negotiable, is a product of personal contract, and owners carry no obligation to sign anything [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:53:18]. The Mississippi heir explainer on Как се прави goes harder still, warning against finders charging up to 10% and telling families to never ever pay a percentage to claim what is already legally theirs [LEhDouSnx9s @ 00:06:24]. Church ties that 50% number directly to the summary administration and probate load on deceased files, not to the cost of finding the heir.

On data, every operator starts with free sites, but they disagree on how bad those sites are and which paid stack wins. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO puts free sites at 50-60% accuracy, refreshed two to three times a year, against BeenVerified at 70-80% pulling every two to three months, and prices Tracers at about $10 setup plus $1.50 per skip or $100-200 monthly packages [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:03:36]. In a separate Unclaimed CEO video, Joe quotes Tracers closer to $1 per skip, pulling daily from 6,000 sources, with BeenVerified around $29 [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:04:30]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 rates free sites lower, around 40-50%, fine for single manual skips but something you graduate from, because once deals come in you are gonna have to pay for bulk data, cold calls and voice drops [Tx1_986LmrY @ 00:01:39]. Skip Matrix COO Shai Korn, on Money Making Juggernaut, pitches a different billing model entirely: a 14-cent maximum per hit paid upfront with misses refunded, a 100-record minimum or a flat $15 below that, no subscription, and a waterfall that runs USPS NCOA before a three-step trace [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:17:09]. Two different Tracers quotes from the same coach show how loosely per-skip pricing gets thrown around.

Pipeline volume splits the room too. Money Making Juggernaut host Eric blast-markets high-surplus properties first and verifies the claim afterward, while others on that call pre-qualify before marketing, and even Eric's own Tennessee claim still took five touches across email, voicemail drop, text, a pause and a follow-up [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:55:08]. The Skipify crew on the same channel pushes raw throughput, telling operators to load anywhere between 150 and 200 properties each week into the system [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:54:19]. Unclaimed CEO's Joe runs the opposite rhythm: five to ten people a week, tops, each worked for 14 to 21 days, hunting a single $7,000-profit lead for two to four weeks, paying the 30-40 cents to mail letters instead of burning out on dial volume, and insisting the data always drives the decision [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:07:48]. On the phones, Joe Green flatly refuses to cold call the dialing-for-dollars way, says operators closing only one or two deals a month are stuck in that mode, and points to the book Smart Calling, official-looking letters, and a monster follow-up that friends the target's family members on social media before sending the target a DM [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:07:04].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest data mistake is tracing the wrong human. Eric of Money Making Juggernaut warns that an address-only lookup returns whoever owns the house now, so it only holds for sales under two months old; anything older needs the prior owner's name uploaded alongside the address [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:29:37]. Even with the right person, phone yield runs thin: one caller reported 25-30% of numbers dead, and Sad from Skipify admitted that of the five numbers returned, four will be wrong, so it is a pure numbers game [aKzRVyO_gfI @ 00:35:15]. Eric says older tracers meant calling 200 people to reach maybe three, and Skip Matrix COO Shai Korn adds that raw county lists arrive broken, with APNs in place of addresses, county and state APNs mixed up, and full names jammed into one column, and confirms Skip Matrix does not suppress previously processed duplicates, while warning that buying TLO data for marketing used to be fine but is not anymore, a real exposure if audited [XEcv7z100aA @ 00:09:58]. Unclaimed CEO's Joe flags the human-side miss: skipping the possible relatives on TruePeopleSearch throws away the people who vouch for you and produce the callbacks that close deals, along with ignoring emails and social media handles entirely [B3w-Sxl2QnE @ 00:02:39].

Heir files die on paperwork, not on skip tracing. GardenShop.Pro states it bluntly: if a single generational link is missing from your paperwork, state auditors will immediately stall or flat-out deny your claim [J2nto2DAwqc @ 00:04:46]. Tamara, the private investigator on Open Book Entrepreneur, works owners deceased 40 to 50 years, which demands a full genealogy and a death certificate for every intermediate heir, and part of their client flow is families who already got denied for missing paperwork [YoID4SzRBaI @ 00:05:40]. David Church saw the rules split by state: California recognized a stepson as heir while Texas denied a stepchild for lacking blood relation, so they now ask up front whether there was a marriage at the time of death, whether there was a will, and whether a marriage-duration rule applies [2l827py8Fe8 @ 00:02:42]. Ohio's division adds hard thresholds: decedent claims under $3,000 move on an unredacted death certificate, marriage or birth certificate and a table of heirship, while $3,000 or more needs a probate order dated within two years and a reopened estate for a newly discovered asset; the 120-day clock only starts once documents are complete, and a claim with no response for 60 days gets dropped and restarts [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:42:53].

The economics only hold when the cost of reaching someone stays small against the check. Joe Green prices Tracers at roughly $1.50 a skip and calls that trivial when ten deals bring in $10,000 to $20,000, but warns that dialing from a personal cell burns it, and that a Missouri number calling Florida gets ignored, so they buy local area codes on Twilio through Nurture Ninja at about $1 per number with a $10 auto-recharging balance [Qf591_R7CN4 @ 00:01:06]. Sean Boujie of SurplusFundsRiches accepts a higher upfront spend on MicroBilt relative and associate mail and messages because it lifts the hit rate 40-50%, and frames the pitch around checking whether someone else is entitled, leaning on Zig Ziglar's point that fear of loss outweighs desire for gain [ujbTh1In_c4 @ 00:02:37]. Church's hard deceased file shows how thin the margin gets: about $14,000 of surplus carries an attorney cost of roughly $1,500 plus 5% alongside the 50% fee they would ask [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:01:31]. Time costs money too: Ohio is running right at three months on review, and the division warns that a finder who initiates a claim pulls the property out of inventory for 60 days [lQrAftswAO4 @ 00:49:32].

chapters.question_prompt: How can operators contact prospects through the channels practitioners demonstrate while addressing scam concerns and calling risks?
chapters.title: Prospect Outreach and Recovery-Service Credibility
chapters.subtitle: Cold-call scripts, phone versus SMS, direct-mail tools, alternatives to cold calling, a seven-deal case study, recovery-letter scrutiny, scam warnings, and DNC-list cautions
chapters.executive_summary: Recovery agents in this niche sell into a trust deficit: state treasuries, the BBB, and consumer-safety channels all tell prospects that claiming is free and that any fee, urgency, or out-of-the-blue contact signals a scam. Practitioners answer with contingency-only terms (David Church pitches 10% with no upfront cost), data-loaded openings that name the payer, address, and dormant date, and legitimacy assets such as websites, QR-coded mailers, and premium business cards. Street mechanics range from Church's phone script and David Wilkerson's slow-intro, KPI-tracked dialing to Eric Richardson's 85-cent Stamp letters and Joe Green's greeting cards, dollar-stuffed mailers, and doorstep envelopes. The sharpest split is cold calling: Wilkerson and Church treat follow-up dials as the job, Green refuses to cold call at all, and Richardson warns that unscrubbed DNC calls drew a federal class action.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every outreach play in this niche starts from a trust deficit, because consumer reporters and the state itself are coaching prospects to hang up. The Pennsylvania Treasurer told FOX43 that a Hollister Scott and Hall letter was 'a little scammy' because it charged $30, plus $5 to expedite, merely to report whether a holding sat under or over $100, information anyone can pull off the Treasury website or get with a phone call [gEVKR-AmaU0 @ 00:00:57]. The BBB of Eastern Oklahoma logged over 800 consumer reports in a single month of a call-and-text twist where victims pay a $50 processing fee and never receive a check [kTrQ-7TzYL4 @ 00:00:33]. Trust Armor lays out the four signals prospects are now trained to listen for: a call out of the blue, manufactured urgency, requests for personal information, and any fee to receive money [8977FkLTYjo @ 00:02:31]. Dark Web Deacon adds that a supposed state agency reaching out by text is an instant tell, and that 'time is running out' language should trigger disengagement [JvMO0OK8kTU @ 00:02:11]. The operator takeaway is blunt: the moves a recovery agent naturally reaches for, meaning cold contact, deadlines, and requests for identity documents, are exactly the moves prospects have been warned about, so legitimacy has to be proven before anything is asked.

The practitioners who actually close deals answer that deficit the same way: nothing out of the client's pocket, a contingency taken only on recovery, and proof-of-legitimacy assets in place before the first touch. David Church of Surplus Institute pitches 'no upfront costs, upon receiving funds we will get 10%, if we don't get you paid you pay nothing at all,' framed as an asset recovery company licensed by the state [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:02:30]. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO tells chamber and BNI networking rooms that searching costs nothing and no fee is charged until the client is paid, after which Green takes a small percentage [zjCP9bHX3oc @ 00:04:03]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut writes 'no upfront fees' and 'free consultation' straight into the mail template, with a QR code routing to a website showing clients already helped [8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:03:18]. Green also treats a website as non-negotiable, even a one-page drag-and-drop build on Go High Level, Wix, or GoDaddy, because people asked for personal documents are guarded and need the operator to 'look and come off reputable' [zjCP9bHX3oc @ 00:06:12]. The common thread is sequencing: prove the money is real and the terms are free-to-start before asking for a single identity document, so the pitch never resembles the fee-first letters regulators keep exposing.

There is equally broad agreement that no single channel carries the load and that persistence is where deals are won. FundSleuth frames outreach as not an either-or choice: email, text, letter writing, and calls all get used, with calling and texting doing the heavy lifting for most prospects [rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:00:37]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101, more than a decade into asset recovery, expects most leads to convert around the third call, says some need a dozen calls or six months of chasing, and notes that the leads demanding the most follow-up tend to carry the biggest paydays [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:14:14]. Joe Green, despite refusing to cold call, reaches the same conclusion from the opposite side: Green says that 90% or more of the time people will not follow up on their own, so the play is to collect their information and chase by text and email, which Green calls 'gold' [97wh_A16P2s @ 00:02:56]. Green's mail logic runs on repetition as well, since a first letter may get no response but prospects who keep hearing from the operator eventually call [WlbnzGtdoSY @ 00:01:06]. Where these operators split is the first touch, not the follow-up; all of them treat the second, third, and twelfth contact as the real work, and Wilkerson names follow-up plus asking for the business as the crucial pair.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: David Church's state-funds script is built on loaded data so the prospect can verify before trusting. Church studies the claim record, then opens: 'This is David Church trying to reach John Smith,' pauses, and names the holder, the street address, and the dormant check, using a California example of a Met Life Insurance check to 235 East 25th Street in Long Beach dated March 1st of 2000, before asking whether the prospect remembers receiving it [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:01:58]. Only after that educating half does the company name come out, followed by the licensed-by-the-state line and the terms: no upfront cost, 10% on success. For deceased owners Church follows the state's order of spouse, then children, then grandchildren, asks about a will, trust, or estate, and expects death certificates, marriage certificates, and sometimes a table of heirship; one such file has run a year and a half [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:02:58]. On 'let me think about it,' Church asks to send the agreements, then asks whether morning or afternoon is better for a follow-up in a couple days, never 'can I call you,' because that question invites a no [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:04:44]. David Wilkerson closes the same way, summarizing the conversation, walking through the contract and notary process, then offering a choice such as Monday afternoon or Monday night [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:10:50].

David Wilkerson's phone mechanics turn on preparation, pace, and measurement. Prep starts the night before: arrive rested with a positive mindset 30 minutes before calling, no drinking or drugs beforehand, no dialing when the operator's mood is off, a quiet workspace with only business tabs open, and a paper pad for notes that later move into the CRM [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:02:27]. On calls Wilkerson leads with questions, uses the ART soft close (ask, restate, tie down), and aims for a calm, late-night-talk-show-host tonality; from shadowing a door-to-door crew, Wilkerson found the top closers' intros ran about three times longer than average [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:08:50]. Daily KPI reports from VAs, kept in free Google Sheets, track dials, talk time, appointments and leads generated, lead incubation time, and contracts signed, with an illustrative ratio of 300 phone calls per contract and one closing per two contracts [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:11:44]. FundSleuth adds the text layer: when a call goes unanswered, still leave the voicemail but follow with an SMS stating who is calling and why, because people read texts far more readily than they listen to voicemails, and use that text only to get the prospect back on the phone, never to negotiate [rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:03:05].

Off the phone, the mechanics get cheap and physical. Eric Richardson sends mail through Stamp at about 73 cents per standard postcard and 85 cents per standard letter at low volume; on 300 leads a month with roughly two addresses per file, because not every skip-traced address is accurate, that is 600 letters for about $510, and one landed surplus deal can pay five figures [8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:01:35]. Joe Green runs greeting cards through a service Green calls Send Out Card, roughly $97 a month for 50 to 100 cards that look handwritten, sometimes stuffing in a real dollar with the line that about 9,000 more are waiting, or a fake $100 bill for laughs [zjCP9bHX3oc @ 00:04:33]. For state-funds leads with sizable accounts inside about a 20-mile radius, Green skips the mailbox and shows up at the door with a black envelope ordered off Amazon and dressed with custom stickers, verifies the name, hands it over, and leaves like 'the FedEx man' [WlbnzGtdoSY @ 00:04:39]. On Facebook, Green friends the lead's friends and relatives first so the lead sees mutual connections and assumes familiarity, then sends the request and works a messenger script once it is accepted [WlbnzGtdoSY @ 00:02:21].
