callout.title: Field-Tested Edges From the Phone, the Inbox, and the Doorstep
callout.body: Small moves the operators credit with turning suspicious pickups and silent leads into signed agreements.
items: When a pickup denies being the owner but probably is, keep feeding the record, including the address, payer, dormant date, and an amount like $1,158, and say the file was assigned; Church reports one heated prospect called back the next day and signed [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:06:11].

Keep the data sheet in front of you on every dial; Church warns that landing on the wrong name forces a call back to redeem yourself, 'and that just never works' [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:05:45].

Green says prospects will not answer a number whose area code differs from theirs, because scammers buy fresh numbers for a dollar and have trained people to ignore strangers [Unclaimed CEO — 97wh_A16P2s @ 00:04:33].

After a call that goes badly, send a text apologizing for getting off on the wrong foot to keep the line of communication alive [FundSleuth - Unclaimed Funds Info and Training — rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:04:10].

sop_steps.title: Load the record before dialing
sop_steps.action: Pull the claim line and keep holder, address, payer, date, and amount on screen for every call.
sop_steps.detail: Church studies the claim before calling and keeps the data in front during the conversation to avoid the wrong-name trap [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:05:32]; Wilkerson keeps only business tabs open and a notepad ready for CRM notes [Surplus Funds 101 — XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:03:10].

sop_steps.title: Open with data, then disclose terms
sop_steps.action: Say the name, the address, and the dormant item, ask if they remember it, then state company and contingency terms.
sop_steps.detail: Church's sequence is name, address, payer, dormant date, then 'an asset recovery company licensed by the state with no upfront cost' and 10% if successful, followed by a pause [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:04:16].

sop_steps.title: Convert missed calls into texts that pull back to the phone
sop_steps.action: Leave the voicemail, send an SMS naming who you are and why, and refuse to negotiate in the thread.
sop_steps.detail: FundSleuth says people read texts more readily than voicemails and that prospects will try to drag the operator into a text negotiation, so the SMS exists only to get the live call [FundSleuth - Unclaimed Funds Info and Training — rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:03:54].

sop_steps.title: Layer mail and track the numbers
sop_steps.action: Test a 100-letter mail batch alongside calls and log every outbound touch daily.
sop_steps.detail: Richardson suggests testing 100 letters for about $85 to see who calls back in [Money Making Juggernaut — 8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:04:30]; Wilkerson says if only one thing gets tracked, track outbound communication: dials, talk time, appointments, incubation time, and contracts signed [Surplus Funds 101 — XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:12:55].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO refuses to cold call and tells students that 90% of their energy belongs in an attraction model, while conceding that cold calling is totally fine for anyone who does not mind it [97wh_A16P2s @ 00:12:41]. Green's own origin story is the counter-case. A first mentor taught skip tracing a 100-prospect list and dialing every lead at least 10 times, which meant more than a thousand calls a week. Most went unanswered, and signed prospects later ghosted or deals fell apart [ie1xaLhl85o @ 00:01:12]. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 sits on the other side of the table. Wilkerson runs outbound dialing with VAs who send a daily KPI report, and quotes a working ratio along the lines of 300 phone calls to land one contract and two contracts per closing [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:11:44]. Wilkerson's case is that outbound communication is the one activity that drives the most revenue, so dials, talk time, appointments, leads generated, lead incubation time, and contracts signed are the numbers to log [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:12:55]. Both camps close on the phone, so the split is not whether phones work. It is whether an operator's hours go into chasing strangers or into a pipeline where prospects arrive already trusting the investigator.

FundSleuth treats text as a credibility tool, never a negotiating table. The play is to send bits of information over SMS to prove the call pertains to the prospect, then steer them onto the phone, because most negotiations are lost over text when it is too easy to say no or simply ghost [rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:01:18]. The FundSleuth sequence is call first. When nobody picks up, leave the voicemail anyway, then send a text explaining who you are and why you called, since people read texts far faster than they listen to voicemails. Joe Green runs the same rule from the inbound side. When a Facebook or LinkedIn group contact connects, never sell the service over text; always schedule a call on the calendar and run the script live [zjCP9bHX3oc @ 00:02:52]. The friction comes from consumer warnings. Amy Mitchell of the Better Business Bureau of Eastern Oklahoma logged more than 800 consumer reports in a single month of a scam that opens with exactly this move: a phone call or text announcing unclaimed funds in the thousands of dollars [kTrQ-7TzYL4 @ 00:00:33]. Dark Web Deacon tells viewers that a text claiming to come from a state government is a quick tell for fraud, and that real asset claims almost always arrive as a letter [JvMO0OK8kTU @ 00:02:32].

Fee framing and urgency split the field just as sharply. David Church of Surplus Institute pitches the firm as a state-licensed asset recovery company with no upfront cost. Church collects 10% only if the funds land, and the claimant pays nothing at all if the claim fails [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:04:16]. Larry K of ShadowAnyone, a private investigator, calls the finder concept a legitimate service, since skip tracers burn time and money on the majority of accounts they fail to locate. Larry K still flags one recovery letter demanding 15% in a state where 10% was the legal maximum the last time Larry looked [VxHOdlFXKdQ @ 00:03:32]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut writes surplus mailers with deliberate urgency. The letter tells former owners the claim is time sensitive and to call before the funds are turned over to the state, and pairs that with a no-upfront-fee line and a QR code to clients already helped [8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:03:04]. Trust Armor teaches the opposite reflex to the same prospects. A contact out of the blue and pressure to act right now or lose the money are two of its four warning signs, and its advice is to hang up and search the official state site independently [8977FkLTYjo @ 00:02:31].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut ran the business from 2018 without a single DNC problem, then got hit with one suit. Richardson had contacted the registered agent of an entity owed a surplus, a realtor whose phone number was public everywhere. The business-to-business carve-out did not stop a federal class action brought by a serial litigator [Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:01:23]. Richardson's attorney laid out the math. Winning would still mean court, depositions, and proving the case, ending with zero paid to the plaintiff but 40,000 in attorney cost [Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:06]. The root cause was blunt: until around September 2024 Richardson was not scrubbing against the Do Not Call list at all, and most skip-tracing providers were not running a DNC check either. The rebuilt stack filters every DNC registrant automatically inside XS Elite, kills voicemail drops and auto dialers, and runs a power dialer one number at a time. A TCPA attorney was paid $3,000 to vet it, and Richardson warns that each state runs its own version of the TCPA [Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:54]. That cuts against the beginner instinct David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 hears constantly: students asking to get on the auto dialer while cold calling is still hard for them to visualize [XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:00:48].

The most painful losses land after the yes. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO describes the worst gut punch in the business. Prospects trust you until you ask for a Social Security card or other identifying documents, and then they get scared. By that point you have coordinated a notary and paid to print and ship the packet, and they ghost [97wh_A16P2s @ 00:13:49]. Green also tracked a student who banked a $30,000 payout, then closed nothing for three months because the pipeline was pure cold calling and no one answered [97wh_A16P2s @ 00:12:30]. David Church of Surplus Institute admits that loaded data does not end the fraud suspicion; people still think it is fraudulent at times. One prospect got really heated on the call, but Church kept sticking to the data, and the prospect called back the next day and the deal closed [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:06:57]. Heir files are the slow-cash trap. Because the state must pay the right person or pay twice, it demands death certificates, marriage certificates, and sometimes a table of heirship. Church's own case on a woman's parents, slowed by destroyed birth records, had run a year and a half without a payout or a denial [wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:03:33].

Credibility can also die on contract terms and letter design. Larry K of ShadowAnyone singles out the last line of one recovery contract, a promise never to authorize any other firm, as a much bigger problem than the fee. Once the form is returned, the claimant must jump through whatever hoops the firm sets and cannot walk to a competitor [VxHOdlFXKdQ @ 00:04:11]. FOX43 News checked the Pennsylvania finder registry for Hollister Scott and Hall, a letter charging $30, plus $5 to expedite, for data pulled straight off the Treasury site. FOX43 found no registration, no website, and no phone number, and the Pennsylvania Treasurer called it scammy but not illegal [gEVKR-AmaU0 @ 00:02:41]. KPRC 2 profiled a homeowner who received a final-notice letter, searched the state unclaimed property site, and found nothing earmarked for the homeowner. That made the homeowner immediately suspicious of the sender, even though the money turned out to be a real homestead refund [a0Bv2mtHL_Y @ 00:00:29]. Eric Richardson's mailer math has its own leak: not every skip-traced address is accurate. That means budgeting roughly two addresses per file, or 600 letters at 85 cents for 300 leads, about $510 a month, to chase a single five-figure surplus claim [8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:01:18].

callout.title: Kill-Switch Checks Before Any Outreach Run Goes Live
callout.body: Four checks pulled from losses the practitioners absorbed firsthand. Any outreach run that cannot clear all four stays parked.
items: Scrub every skip-traced number against the DNC list before a single dial, call one number at a time on a power dialer, and run no voicemail drops or auto-blast dialing; one unscrubbed contact turned into a federal class action [Money Making Juggernaut — Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:21].

Check the contingency percentage against the state cap before an agreement goes out, and strip any clause barring the claimant from using another firm; a 15% letter was flagged in a state with a 10% maximum [ShadowAnyone — VxHOdlFXKdQ @ 00:03:32].

Have a live, professional website before asking for a Social Security card or ID documents, because prospects who cannot verify the investigator ghost after the notary and shipping money is already spent [Unclaimed CEO — 97wh_A16P2s @ 00:14:01].

Where the state runs a finder registry, be on it before mailing; FOX43 pulled the Pennsylvania registry and named Hollister Scott and Hall on air as an unregistered finder [FOX43 News — gEVKR-AmaU0 @ 00:02:41].

chapters.pull_quote: "Hey, I didn't pay the guy a dime, but then I paid 40,000 in attorney cost." — Eric Richardson, attributed to Money Making Juggernaut (Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:06).
action_checklist: Run an automated DNC filter on every skip-traced list, then dial one number at a time on a power dialer with no voicemail drops or auto dialers [Money Making Juggernaut — Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:21].

Open every call with the claimant's name, the property address, the holder, the date, and the amount, and keep that data in front of you for the entire conversation [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:00:27].

When a call goes unanswered, leave the voicemail, then text who you are and why you called, and use the SMS only to get the prospect back on the phone [FundSleuth - Unclaimed Funds Info and Training — rQqA2wnJ9xw @ 00:03:05].
Test 100 printed letters at 85 cents each, about $85 total, with a QR code that sends prospects to your website to see clients you have helped [Money Making Juggernaut — 8hCl2lLNDrk @ 00:04:30].

When a prospect says let me think about it, offer to send the agreements and ask whether morning or afternoon is better for the follow-up call [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — wp5vC44yQQg @ 00:04:30].

Log dials, talk time, appointments, leads generated, lead incubation time, and contracts signed in a free Google Sheet, and keep following up well past the third call [Surplus Funds 101 — XHOqG0CY1KA @ 00:12:55].

chapters.question_prompt: How do practitioners move from a recovery opportunity to an agreement, claim, and collected fee, and what operating problems arise along the way?
chapters.title: Close Claims and Collect Recovery Fees
chapters.subtitle: Reported state-fund recoveries and finder fees, county funds and tax overages, claimant willingness, attorney searches, client checks, CRM use, contract disputes, and false compliance notices
chapters.executive_summary: Closers across Money Making Juggernaut, Unclaimed CEO, Surplus Institute, and Spring Solutions agree the fee is won by never asking for money up front, looking like a legitimate firm, and following up until paperwork comes back signed. The mechanics are tight: a contract with an approximate amount and a percentage, a notarized power of attorney, and only the filing documents the county requests. Numbers run from Eric Richardson's $150 flat packet on $500 to $8,000 county claims and 15% to 30% contingency above $10,000, to David Church's 10% state-fund cut ($5,400 on $54,000) and 40% on a paperwork-heavy estate overage. Jay's interest clause lifted one New Jersey estate fee from $18,000 to $31,000. Collection runs through a professional invoice and a cashier's check. When a client stiffs the finder, Spring Porter runs a 10-day letter, a small-claims complaint, a judgment, and garnishment.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every closer here sells the same hook: the client pays nothing until the check lands. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO tells investigators not to ask for any money until the client is paid first, then to take a percentage of the total claim. Green scripts the close as 'no money out of pocket, if you don't get paid I don't get paid, do you want to do business' [ug2uUK_s2yk @ 00:05:39]. Green frames the psychology like eating out. People know how to cook, yet they pay more to skip the work. When the service is done as a courtesy up front and payment waits until after the client is paid, people start to trust and like the investigator, because nobody asked for a credit card [bAARnig4bT4 @ 00:01:20]. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut drops the same promise into the state-funds call right after confirming identity: 'I charge no upfront fees and I take care of all filing costs.' Richardson then collects the email address to send proof [bfDePAnN-4Y @ 00:05:38]. Green concedes that a few people will file alone once they learn about the money, but calls them few and far between. Most will split their funds so they can get back to their kids, jobs, or school while someone else handles the signatures and the follow-through [bAARnig4bT4 @ 00:01:49]. Take away the upfront ask and the paperwork comes back signed.

The second point of agreement: fees get collected by operators who look like a real firm, not a stranger with a phone. Jay is the Money Making Juggernaut student who banked $31,000 on one New Jersey estate claim. Jay lists the stack bluntly: a professional website, professional emails, a business bank account, and an LLC, 'because you can't be John Doe just calling someone.' Jay adds that prospects routinely ask whether a website exists [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:12:20]. Joe Green pushes the same build order. Get an EIN from the IRS, file with the state, register with the county where required, get a city business license, build a website, and set up a Google business listing so prospects can verify the outfit before signing anything [bAARnig4bT4 @ 00:03:39]. David Church of Surplus Institute ties professionalism directly to getting paid after the client receives the money first. Come off as a professional who has worked the case, keep in touch while the claim is pending, then send a professional-looking invoice [kb-pXZgQdoE @ 00:00:27]. Richardson adds the licensing layer before any outreach. Check each state for registered-finder rules, fingerprinting, private investigator requirements, mandated agreement disclosures, no-contact waiting periods, and fee caps of 10%, 20%, or 30% [bfDePAnN-4Y @ 00:01:29]. Green warns that a missed registration often surfaces only when the claim paperwork is filed, after the deal is already made.

Practitioners agree the big fees are won by patience and relentless follow-up, not one call. Jay spent roughly five months on a skeptical older client whose identity had been stolen before. Jay called about once a week, talked golf, sports, and health remedies, and told the client, 'I'm going to become your friend first,' until the client said they were ready to move forward [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:06:07]. Jay's rule on stalled prospects is to keep texting and calling even when people get tired of hearing from you, because the tenth touch can close after nine misses. One holiday brush-off was chased from Thanksgiving through New Year's Eve and became an $8,000 take-home deal [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:09:35]. David Church earned the trust of an elderly heir in their mid-eighties by asking to speak with the heir's own daughter. That daughter later called back and said they had assumed it was fraud, but now fully trusted David precisely because David asked for family [pOEq9UMUFHU @ 00:02:26]. Richardson's CRM pipeline enforces the same discipline on hard-to-locate leads. Call again the next day, use every number skip tracing turns up, search social media, neighbors, and relatives, send a mailer, and make a final reach-out before deleting the lead, because 'this is a numbers game' [ZsII5-XkqPY @ 00:07:07].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The filing package that turns a yes into a payable claim is short. Joe Green names three minimum documents. The first is a contract signed by both sides that states an approximate recovery amount, because other liens may cut into the total, along with the finder-fee percentage. The second is a power of attorney, which must be notarized. The third is the county's own filing documents, sending only what the instructions request so the claim processes faster [pZG8hK4VPVM @ 00:00:30]. Green pre-fills the client's basic information, mails the package, and sends a mobile notary to the client's house or a public spot so the client doesn't no-show. Green then charges the notary fee on the back end [pZG8hK4VPVM @ 00:01:44]. Eric Richardson cautions that some states require specific contract language; Colorado, for example, requires certain literature on the agreement form. The proof Richardson sends is simply the client's name highlighted on the state list, plus the statute so the client can search for themselves [bfDePAnN-4Y @ 00:05:53]. At the county level, Richardson says the claim is a one-page form: claim form, proof of ID, and a notary appointment, all doable in under an hour. The client is sent to their bank, Amscot, FedEx, or UPS to notarize for about $15 [xocEKVSCJtU @ 00:09:07].

Pricing flexes with claim size and paperwork burden. Eric Richardson runs two county models. Larger claims of roughly $10,000 and up go on contingency at 15% to 30% through an agreement form. Claims from $500 to about $8,000 go through a 'packet process,' with a flat $150 charge to inform the client and prepare the claim documents [xocEKVSCJtU @ 00:08:13]. The upfront route is about volume, since small claims rarely justify waiting on a contingency. Richardson invoices through PayPal, Stripe, Square, or a Googled template and gets paid before doing the service, insisting that simply informing someone of unclaimed money is valuable because counties do almost nothing to notify owners [xocEKVSCJtU @ 00:09:53]. On state funds David Church takes 10%, the allowed amount on the $54,000 claim that produced a $5,400 cashier's check [kb-pXZgQdoE @ 00:00:57]. Church prices up for difficulty. One roughly $15,000 Florida overage was owed to the son of a deceased 98-year-old owner; the son had never moved the property into their own name and believed the funds were uncollectable. Church set 40% with the client keeping 60%, nearly went higher because of the paperwork, and still expected north of $4,000 after a few hundred dollars in lawyer fees [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:03:17].

Collection itself is a contract-and-paper game. Jay wrote an interest clause into the agreement, so any interest that accrued while the funds sat at the state treasury also fell under the agreed percentage. The mother's account grew from $155,000 to $185,000 over 30 to 35 years, which pushed an expected $18,000 cut to $31,000. That took about 12 hours of work, which Richardson pegs at over $2,700 an hour [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:04:22]. David Church gets the client paid first, then sends a professional invoice for the agreed amount and receives a cashier's check back by mail, which Church says happens all day long [kb-pXZgQdoE @ 00:01:11]. When a client stiffs the finder, Spring Porter of Spring Solutions lays out a self-represented small-claims path. Confirm the statute of limitations, which is three years on a Maryland contract, and gather the signed contract, invoice, and emails. Send a 10-day letter, then file a complaint with interrogatories, serve it through the sheriff or a process server, and push to default judgment and then garnishment or a lien [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:03:06]. Porter's own $1,100 Virginia holdout called once a suit was threatened and agreed to $400 down and $150 a month, papered as a promissory note. Porter notes that bankruptcy petitions on PACER list employers and banks for garnishment [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:07:57].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is how the fee gets priced and when it gets collected. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut runs two parallel county playbooks: a contingency agreement at 15% to 30% on claims of roughly $10,000 and up, and a flat $150 packet process on claims between $500 and about $8,000, invoiced through PayPal, Stripe, or Square before any work starts, because informing people of unclaimed funds is itself valuable [xocEKVSCJtU @ 00:08:13]. David Church of Surplus Institute prices by difficulty instead: on a roughly $15,000 Florida overage owed to a deceased father's estate, David came in at 40% because of the paperwork involved, leaving the son 60% [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:03:32]. On state funds, David took a straight 10%, a $5,400 cashier's check on a $54,000 claim, the share David says they are allowed to get [kb-pXZgQdoE @ 00:00:57]. Jay, a Money Making Juggernaut student, took about $1,500 on the son's own $7,000 claim, then wrote the mother's estate contract so the agreed percentage also applied to any interest the funds accumulated. A $155,000 balance that had sat with the New Jersey treasury since the 1980s grew to $185,000, and Jay's cut jumped from a projected $18,000 to $31,000 [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:04:00]. That clause alone added roughly $13,000 to one check.

Practitioners also split on who carries the notary and how much paper goes to the clerk. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO pre-fills the client's basic information, mails the documents, and sends a mobile notary to the client's house or a public place where they feel comfortable, then charges the notary fee on the back end so the client never has to arrange anything [pZG8hK4VPVM @ 00:01:44]. Eric Richardson pushes that step onto the client on $150 packet deals, sending them to their bank, Amscot, FedEx, or UPS, where notarizing might cost $15, rather than paying a notary out of the $150 [xocEKVSCJtU @ 00:09:24]. On filing volume, Joe Green warns that many online teachers stuff claims with unnecessary documents the county already holds: 'just give them what they're asking for so they can process the claim faster' [pZG8hK4VPVM @ 00:02:23]. David Church lived the opposite case on a state claim where the will had burned in a house fire. The state denied, the state advocate denied, and David traded more than 30 emails while pushing the heir for tax records, CPA files, old bank statements, and old emails before an affidavit backed by birth and death certificates finally moved the claim [pOEq9UMUFHU @ 00:04:21].

The attorney question splits the room. Eric Richardson calls an attorney 'your best friend' in this business: for probate on deceased owners, for interpleader fights, for counties that will not work with third-party companies, and for closing skeptical clients who can look up a bar license. Eric steers students toward contingent attorneys whose cost runs up to about $8,000 on the high end [zrj6RA8N9HA @ 00:05:14]. Spring Porter of Spring Solutions takes the do-it-yourself line on collecting a stiffed fee. On an $1,100 Virginia bankruptcy unclaimed funds deal, Spring refused to pay an attorney four or five hundred dollars when the county website lists every form, and warns that lawyers 'don't always have the best case management,' missing process server certificates, forgetting promissory notes, and stopping at judgment without hunting assets [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:11:50]. David Church splits the difference, budgeting a few hundred dollars of lawyer fees on a difficult Florida estate overage and still expecting to net north of $4,000 [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:04:50]. On pace, Jay spent months befriending a skeptical elderly client with weekly calls before any paperwork moved, while David refuses to chase anyone who wants to go around: 'I don't want to beg people for the business' [pOEq9UMUFHU @ 00:01:56].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest failure is the client who gets the check and never pays. Spring Porter of Spring Solutions hit exactly that on an $1,100 Virginia bankruptcy unclaimed funds file and laid out the escalation: a 10-day demand letter, then a small claims complaint with the signed contract, invoice, and emails attached as exhibits, service by sheriff or process server, a hearing or default judgment, and finally garnishment of a bank account or employer or a lien on property [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:03:22]. The threat alone worked for Spring: once the letter was announced, the client called and set up $400 down and $150 a month on a promissory note [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:07:57]. Spring also reports debtors who ignore service and even the judgment, which forces post-judgment skip tracing, with the old bankruptcy petition on PACER serving as a starting map of employers, banks, and property [2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:09:19]. David Church shows the preventive version: present as a professional who has worked the case, keep in touch with the client through a four-month claim, and send a professional-looking invoice for the amount owed, which brought back a $5,400 cashier's check [kb-pXZgQdoE @ 00:00:41].

Claims also die inside the file. On David Church's daughter-heir state claim, tax records, CPA files, old bank branches, and old emails all came up empty after the will burned; the affidavit route got the daughter only one third of the claim, and the state sent the other two thirds to the deceased siblings' children [pOEq9UMUFHU @ 00:05:34]. The clock kills more deals. Joe Green of Unclaimed CEO says that in most cases counties have 365 days to find the owner before the money goes to the state or into the next fiscal year budget, while some Florida counties hold surplus only about three months [ug2uUK_s2yk @ 00:03:04]. Grant of Overage Acquisition is blunt about the stakes: if the prior homeowner never files with specific documentation, the equity is forfeited to the county or state, and 'they get to keep it' [La2LN9HMPbs @ 00:04:34]. David's Florida overage on a deceased 98-year-old owner was about to go to the state, so David tried every number, individually skip traced a relative, and reached the son on the very last listed phone [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:01:07]. The son first told David the funds were uncollectible because the property was never moved into the son's name.

Trust and fraud cut both ways. Jay's New Jersey client had had personal information stolen before, which Jay calls grounds to hang up on any caller; closing took months of patient calls, about five months of processing, and roughly 12 hours of on-and-off work that Eric Richardson prices at over $2,700 per hour [ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:05:27]. On the government side, Lynn Hall, manager of DC's unclaimed property unit, says COVID brought bad actors and a lot of fraud, so DC stopped mailing fast-track checks directly and created its own fraud unit, and under the Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act of 2021 heir finders face a fee cap and lost access to full owner lists [xfSFTtM1yT8 @ 00:18:36]. Joe Green warns operators not to start making deals and then discover at filing that they never registered in a state that requires it [bAARnig4bT4 @ 00:05:15]. David Church flags an overhead trap aimed at operators themselves: a 'Corporate Compliance Center' notice from a Sacramento address demanding $179 for entity, officer, and payment details while never asking for minutes, and 'these guys are not going to show up at your audit and defend you' [gitQwM01Fgc @ 00:05:08].

callout.title: Clear These Before You File or Invoice
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, stall, or near-miss a practitioner hit firsthand at the close-and-collect stage.
items: Signed contract, invoice, and every email saved before the claim is filed, because Spring Porter had to attach all three as lawsuit exhibits and works inside a three-year Maryland window to sue on a contract [Spring Solutions, LLC — 2Q7vcVR_cDs @ 00:02:50].

State registration confirmed before the first cold call, because Joe Green warns against closing deals and then finding out at filing that registration was skipped [Unclaimed CEO — bAARnig4bT4 @ 00:05:03].
Contract wording covers accrued interest on the held funds, because Jay's interest clause raised one fee from $18,000 to $31,000 [Money Making Juggernaut — ZvJ4yCc9em4 @ 00:04:22].

No payment sent to unsolicited compliance notices, because David Church's $179 Corporate Compliance Center letter asked for officer and payment details and never for minutes [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — gitQwM01Fgc @ 00:03:10].

action_checklist: Before marketing, check each state's rules on registered finder or PI status, required agreement disclosures, no-contact waiting periods, and fee caps of 10%, 20%, or 30% [Money Making Juggernaut — bfDePAnN-4Y @ 00:02:15].

Close by emailing proof (the client's name highlighted on the state list) plus an agreement form carrying any state-specific language, such as Colorado's required wording [Money Making Juggernaut — bfDePAnN-4Y @ 00:05:53].
Build the filing package from a signed contract, a notarized power of attorney, and only the documents the county's filing instructions require [Unclaimed CEO — pZG8hK4VPVM @ 00:02:53].

For clients who don't use computers, mail the documents physically and schedule the notary yourself instead of waiting on an e-signature [Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds — V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:04:12].

chapters.question_prompt: How do practitioners find and verify bankruptcy unclaimed funds, navigate court-specific issues, and evaluate fees and payout examples?
chapters.title: Bankruptcy Unclaimed Funds Recovery
chapters.subtitle: U.S. Courts locator searches, claims registers, fund-amount discrepancies, creditor-claim difficulties, Florida districts, U.S. territories, finder fees, and practitioner payout cases
chapters.executive_summary: Eric Richardson, Will Whitman, Darius, and Spring Porter describe a recovery business built around bankruptcy payments that never reached their owners. The operating sequence is concrete: locate a balance, identify the entitled party, research the docket, explain the money, secure the agreement, and submit the court's documents. Richardson promotes centralized leads and a $300 monthly platform; Porter demonstrates district-specific searches, claims-register research, and persistent follow-up. Their economics range from Porter's smaller stacked commissions to Richardson's guest accepting 20% on a recovery slightly above $34,000. The contrasts matter: centralized searches omit districts, actual payouts can exceed Richardson's 30–60-day expectation, and Porter's finder-fee discussion raises state-level contract concerns alongside the speakers' emphasis on negotiation. Documented ownership, court-specific paperwork, and claimant follow-through drive the work.

sections.title: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The business starts with a payment that failed to reach its owner, not with a promise that every bankruptcy produces a windfall. Eric Richardson describes closed cases with undistributed money, incorrect addresses, deceased recipients, and checks that somebody simply never claimed. The debtor is the party in debt; the creditor is the party entitled to payment on that debt. Those roles matter before any outreach because the money can belong to either side [EyQovsqVOnE @ 00:00:28]. Darius at ACE SURPLUS gives the same basic picture: a distribution cannot be delivered, a check remains uncashed, and the payment returns as unclaimed funds. Individuals and companies can be recipients, and a debtor can receive a refund [daCZb9lQvnc @ 00:00:28]. Will Whitman frames the operator's job as identifying people separated from their money and bringing the two back together, whether the person filed the bankruptcy or participated as a creditor [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:03:36]. Richardson's practical sequence is research, skip tracing, marketing, contracting, and claim submission. The research must explain how the funds arose, because a person whose bankruptcy ended years ago may reject the premise immediately. Reading the docket is part of being able to explain the claim professionally, not just a way to collect another name for a calling list [EyQovsqVOnE @ 00:02:31].

The shared starting point is a searchable court balance followed by case research, but the national locator is not the whole inventory. Whitman describes a database sortable by amount and filterable by court, estimating participation at roughly 95% and suggesting a focused Northern District of Georgia search for claims between $10,000 and $20,000 [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:10:05]. Darius also directs searchers to the online registry while estimating 90% coverage and saying the missing courts require direct contact [daCZb9lQvnc @ 00:04:22]. Spring Porter supplies the concrete district example: Western District of Missouri used its own PDF with more than 400 cases rather than appearing in the locator [ckzrLZgtcYI @ 00:03:12]. That means the district's own information remains part of the search work, even when the main locator makes national prospecting convenient. Richardson then separates locating a listing from establishing its current status. In PACER, the operator checks whether somebody submitted a claim, whether payment followed, and whether the filing covered only part of the balance. Richardson and Whitman also report encountering a false claim, so an application appearing in the docket is not their signal to automatically abandon the lead. Their instruction is to read what happened and determine whether money remains rather than treating every existing filing as the end of the opportunity [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:15:14].

The service pitch rests on explaining the record and handling the paperwork, not merely announcing that money exists. Richardson recommends sending the documentary proof with an introductory email, alongside the company's website and email identity. Whitman identifies the trustee's report of deposit as the written record produced when unclaimed money enters the court [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:12:04]. Richardson's guest makes the same point from actual conversations: understanding the bankruptcy lets the caller explain where the money came from, which makes the service easier for a claimant to understand and accept [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:04:11]. Porter describes the work as researching leads, contacting prospective clients, and preparing documents for filing; the scripts, letters, and contracts support that sequence rather than replacing it [CJMCHDgNh4M @ 00:01:54]. Baseline preparation also includes learning the receiving court's process. Darius says ACE SURPLUS handles application preparation and filing, emphasizes each court's administrative process, and points to errors as a reason clients experience delays or denials [daCZb9lQvnc @ 00:03:22]. These practitioners sell the ability to connect the claimant, the documented balance, and the required submission. A name and amount provide a lead; the conversation needs the explanation, and the filing needs the forms. That is the common service underneath Richardson's marketing system, Porter's document work, and Darius's application-handling offer.

sections.title: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: For a focused lead search, use Whitman's district-and-amount example: Northern District of Georgia, $10,000–$20,000 claims. Richardson also describes sorting fresh entries above $10,000 or ordering balances from highest to lowest [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:10:25]. For a broad personal search, Badwolf recommends leaving the court field empty and running the name separately as creditor and debtor, with case number and time frame left open when those details are not being used [suC7b2tuNcc @ 00:05:00]. Porter demonstrates a different route in Eastern New York, where the district's search requires a case number, debtor name, or creditor name. Entering bank names, or simply 'bank,' produces creditor leads; the example selected is a $31,802 Citibank balance [5A3cah6ujY4 @ 00:02:03]. Porter tries CourtListener first, finds that the case does not appear, and moves to PACER. There, the sequence is Find Cases, docket report, the unclaimed-funds entry near the bottom, and then the claims register. The Citibank filing is claim number three; its supporting document identifies the person who filed and provides a telephone number. Porter treats that as a contact lead while acknowledging the employee may no longer be there. The document also supplies supporting information for the recovery application [5A3cah6ujY4 @ 00:05:37].

Richardson's tool-assisted route combines skip tracing and documentary proof inside Bankruptcy Surplus. Richardson names BeenVerified and Skip Matrix as other research options, then describes the platform's phone numbers, relatives' details, email addresses, social links, and notice-of-deposit documents [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:16:48]. The marketing stack includes calls, texts, voicemail drops, emails, and follow-up triggers; Richardson reports four to five incoming calls per day and describes asking interested callers for an email address so the proof can be sent immediately [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:18:33]. Porter supplies the manual follow-through. When a client returned something signed but omitted another requirement, Porter texted a photograph of the signed contract and used casual language to remind the client that the remaining documents were still needed. Porter also suggests asking about Facebook as another communication route [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:02:05]. The CRM must include prospects, not only signed clients: Porter recounts forgetting earlier mailings and being caught unprepared when recipients called back. Record working and nonworking numbers, email, preferred communication, case information, the fund amount, and the agreed percentage. Porter specifically warns against remembering a different fee than the one originally discussed. Those notes let the operator resume the actual conversation rather than ask the returning prospect what was offered [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:03:26].

The economics are negotiated percentages on particular recoveries, with different operators choosing different deal sizes. Richardson quotes Bankruptcy Surplus at $300 monthly and describes 30–60 days as the ideal payment window, while noting that probate and additional work can extend it [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:27:36]. Richardson's guest accepted 20% on a straightforward recovery slightly above $34,000, but reports three or four months for the New York process, including a court Zoom call and successive processing periods of 21–35 days [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:07:14]. Porter shows the smaller-deal version: a 30% fee on $1,117.83 in Western Missouri produced $335.34, and that recovery joined Alabama and an earlier Virginia deal in a combined $1,030.14 commission total. Porter estimates about an hour of work, including travel, notarization, copies, and mailing, while explicitly separating that work from the waiting time [ckzrLZgtcYI @ 00:02:52]. On pricing, Porter urges negotiation rather than losing a client over a demand for half the recovery. Porter describes starting high and settling somewhere in the middle, and explains that 35% or 40% will not always be accepted. The specific tactic is to discuss the work being performed and adjust the percentage instead of treating the opening request as immovable [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:07:01].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Eric Richardson sells bankruptcy recovery as a centralized alternative to hunting county foreclosure lists: one site supplies names, amounts, and court locations, then the operator researches the case. Will Whitman narrows that pitch in their webinar, estimating that the locator covers about 95% of bankruptcy courts rather than every court; they also describe filtering a particular district for claims between $10,000 and $20,000 [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:10:05]. Darius at ACE SURPLUS gives a different coverage estimate, saying 90% of courts appear and that missing courts require direct contact [daCZb9lQvnc @ 00:04:22]. Spring Porter demonstrates what searching beyond the central locator actually involves. In Florida, Porter finds only the Southern District listed, then visits the Northern and Middle District websites separately. The Northern District offers application paperwork and an affidavit, while the Middle District calls for a motion; the same state does not mean identical filing mechanics [R8PpcOrRZc4 @ 00:07:24]. Porter also searches territories: Puerto Rico appears in the locator, Guam has a separate PDF, and other territory searches lead to clerk contacts. Puerto Rico introduces a practical language barrier: Porter encounters Spanish court documents despite English search pages and describes discovering that difficulty firsthand. These are alternative lead routes, not completed territory recoveries [lWmrc3x-B-E @ 00:02:42].

Fee advice splits between negotiated percentages and Porter's warning about what happens when a client relationship becomes a contract dispute. Richardson answers the webinar's fee-cap question by saying the percentage is discretionary and negotiable, immediately adding that asking for 50% or 60% does not mean the client will accept it [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:28:49]. Porter likewise tells operators to negotiate rather than abandon a claim because the owner will not surrender half. Porter recounts contacting someone whose earlier locator wanted half and would not negotiate, and describes starting high before settling somewhere in the middle [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:07:01]. But Porter's dedicated finder-fee discussion takes a different position on state rules: absence of fee language in bankruptcy materials does not, in Porter's account, remove state-level exposure when a deal turns into litigation. Porter describes considering an $1,100 Virginia contract suit against a client who had not paid, without reporting a court victory [sf-f4iZbpRo @ 00:06:45]. Richardson's interview guest supplies a completed-deal comparison: a claim worth a little more than $34,000 carried an agreed 20% company fee because the case was straightforward. That figure describes the recovered claim, not a $34,000 take-home commission. The guest's rationale was accepting a worthwhile fee rather than pushing for more [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:07:14].

The outreach playbooks range from a paid operating system to ordinary calls and self-directed name searches. Richardson describes Bankruptcy Surplus as a database with skip-traced contacts, supporting documents, a CRM, and claim processing; the webinar prices that service at $300 monthly. Operators can market inside the system and request filing when a prospect is ready, while the course also teaches independent research and filing [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:26:51]. Richardson's interview guest reports a simpler acquisition method: calling. Their partnership divides calls and paperwork, but several identified owners still procrastinate, including contacts associated with $232,000 and $65,000 claims. The guest keeps checking whether those owners have filed and offers help again [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:05:47]. Porter favors text follow-up when contracts return incomplete, sometimes sending a photograph of the signed contract and using conversational language. Porter also asks about Facebook and records how clients prefer to communicate [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:02:05]. Badwolf Unincorporated takes a different route entirely: search for yourself or relatives, leave the court field empty, and run the name separately as creditor and debtor. Badwolf's broad search produces many similar names, followed by suggestions to request identifying information. That demonstration is personal discovery and inquiry, not a reported paid recovery operation [suC7b2tuNcc @ 00:05:00].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Porter's Missouri discrepancy shows why a listed amount can stall the entire job. A district PDF showed $1,983, while the trustee's final report showed more than $13,000. Porter found repeated deposit entries and withdrawals, could not reconcile the figures, and pursued clarification because the larger commission made the extra work worthwhile [y2j1Ux0R9jY @ 00:01:08]. The bankruptcy clerk could not resolve it; the trustee's office also struggled; a judge's law clerk redirected Porter to the courtroom deputy. Porter left a message rather than reporting a resolved balance. Porter explicitly declined to contact the owner and prepare an application with an amount that might be wrong, and contemplated moving on if nobody answered [y2j1Ux0R9jY @ 00:04:48]. Another amount trap appears in Porter's Northern Florida walkthrough: a displayed case total of roughly $2,300 was divided among five creditors, rather than belonging to one claimant. Opening the case exposed the individual allocations [R8PpcOrRZc4 @ 00:03:32]. Richardson and Whitman add a different docket trap: they encountered a false claim, and Richardson explains that an existing application does not automatically exhaust the funds. Their research includes whether payment occurred or whether somebody sought only a portion. The job is to understand the entries, not simply abandon every docket containing a claim [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:15:32].

Payout timing and headline earnings diverge sharply across the reported jobs. Richardson describes 30 to 60 days as an ideal payout window, with additional proceedings such as probate potentially extending it [NxCoaATrtq4 @ 00:28:30]. The interview guest's completed New York claim instead took about three or four months, including a court Zoom verification and successive processing intervals described as 21 to 35 days. The same guest reports two Texas filings delayed by a six-month backlog with one person handling the work; an Illinois filing had been accepted, but its anticipated payout had not arrived [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:02:30] [waps0YmW8BI @ 00:08:13]. Porter supplies another concrete timeline: a Middle District of Alabama claim submitted September 30 produced a check dated January 7. Porter's fee there was $294.80 at 40%, while the Western District of Missouri example produced a $335.34 fee at 30%. Porter describes Missouri as fast and Alabama as slow despite friendly staff and easy paperwork. The $1,030.14 headline combines those fees with an earlier Eastern District of Virginia deal; Porter estimates about an hour of work but explicitly says there was waiting and that this was not daily income. Some districts mailed checks rather than sending electronic transfers [ckzrLZgtcYI @ 00:00:32].

Institutional access and unfinished client paperwork create bottlenecks before payment processing even begins. Porter contacted Georgia's Department of Revenue about $9,718 still sitting in a court registry, returned after an earlier January call, and reached a representative who lacked authority. The manager was unavailable, leaving another message rather than a signed engagement. Porter describes government creditors as difficult to reach through someone who understands the recovery request [1fuOy7IsEMo @ 00:00:31]. In the Eastern District of New York walkthrough, Porter researches a $31,802 Citibank entry through PACER and the claims register, locating the original claim signer's telephone number. Porter does not report collecting that money and says banking contacts have promised to investigate, then failed to return calls [5A3cah6ujY4 @ 00:09:31]. Smaller administrative failures are just as explicit: Porter has forgotten prospects after mailing them, struggled to remember quoted percentages, and received signed contracts with missing notarization. The response is to record prospects and communication preferences, retain fee notes, and follow up on missing documents. Sending identification separately can also trigger a deficiency notice when a clerk expects one package [YKjd__UIhB8 @ 00:00:50]. Darius at ACE SURPLUS identifies filing errors as a source of client delays and denials, making document preparation a central part of the service [daCZb9lQvnc @ 00:03:42].

callout.title: Resolve the amount, the paperwork, and the payout record
callout.body: Porter's operating checks address conflicting balances, incomplete submissions, forgotten prospects, and incorrect client distributions.
items: Resolve a material balance discrepancy before approaching the owner with that amount. Porter pursued the clerk, trustee's office, and courtroom deputy rather than preparing a claim around an unresolved figure. [Spring Solutions, LLC — y2j1Ux0R9jY @ 00:06:02]

chapters.question_prompt: What specialized recovery and reporting workflows are demonstrated for royalties, insurance proceeds, shares, and dividends?
chapters.title: Royalties, Insurance, Shares, and Dividends
chapters.subtitle: Oil-and-gas royalty searches and holder workflows, life-insurance policy tracing, demutualization funds, insurance payouts, Indian IEPFA searches, and Nigerian share and dividend recovery
chapters.executive_summary: Royalty, insurance, share, and dividend money escheats on the same mechanic everywhere: a dormancy clock (3 years for Texas MI02 royalties, 3-5 years for most insurance, 7 consecutive years before Indian shares move to the IEPFA, 6 years before Nigerian dividends hit the trust fund), and then a state or statutory custodian holds it. Practitioners agree the search is free and must be run across every state, portal, and registrar. Death, moves, and undisclosed assets drive most losses. Street mechanics center on name-variant searches, operator and registrar identification, ID-plus-BVN or PAN packets, and probate or heirship proof. Texas caps finder fees at 10%, MIB charges $75, and Nigerian claims can pay the same day. The split is between DIY filers and paid services from Enterslice, Broadstreet's firm, and lawyers like Daggett Shuler.

key_metrics.label: Texas Finder Fee Cap
key_metrics.value: 10% of what's recovered
key_metrics.context: Texas law caps the finder fee at 10%, with no share of minerals, overriding royalty, or production payment. The agreement must be written, the finder cannot file the claim, and the finder must hold a DPS license.

key_metrics.context: The host attributes the rise to new dividends and new market entrants, and says the money earns no interest while 'the banks are feeding fat on it.'

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner across the four asset classes describes the same machine: money stops moving, a dormancy clock runs, and the holder ships the balance to a government custodian. On the oil side, Royalty Clerk lays out a five-stop path. A check is returned or never cashed. Royalties sit unclaimed for more than 3 years after becoming payable. A notice goes out if the amount tops $250 and an address exists. The company then delivers the money to the Comptroller by July 1 [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:00:52]. The txcomptroller holder training gives the code-level version: MI02 royalties go abandoned after 3 years of inactivity and MS01 wages after 1 year, with the clock starting at the most recent of last contact, check issue, or payable date [rGLI7Ry3sF0 @ 00:01:45]. The PakEnergy panel puts typical dormancy at 3-5 years, with Louisiana at 2 and Ohio at 1, and flags date of death as a new trigger [fVMIbCz8s0U @ 00:19:42]. The Indian dividend version is faster and harsher. The Mint segment explains that dividends must be encashed within 30 days and then move to an unpaid dividend account. After 7 consecutive unclaimed years, the underlying shares themselves transfer to the IEPFA [Y4d3T6BNtEg @ 00:01:31].

The causes repeat almost word for word across royalties, dividends, and insurance. Royalty Clerk lists moves, unreported deaths, name changes, and tiny uncashed checks. He warns that later royalties keep following the first payment to the state until the address is fixed [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:01:12]. Blue Mesa Minerals adds the operator-side reasons money lands in suspense before it ever escheats: unsigned division orders, heirship that was never transferred, title defects, and lawsuits [HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:00:21]. On the Nigerian dividend side, the Broadstreet Radio host says most unclaimed dividends belong to dead people who hid their wealth from family. His blunt fix is to disclose your assets to your family while you are alive [DLhQH9iGJ84 @ 00:01:03]. The insurance demutualization explainer from Как се прави describes the institutional half of the same failure. Insurers skipped Death Master File checks, which triggered multi-state audits, and non-electing policyholders ended up with stock parked at transfer agents [oUFeGA0MPoM @ 00:04:53]. The pattern the practitioners describe is consistent: a person died, moved, or never told anyone, and the paper trail stopped at the holder's desk. That makes death records, old addresses, and family knowledge the real search keys.

The strongest point of agreement is that the search itself costs nothing and should be run wide, not once. Royalty Clerk stresses that searching the Texas database is free, takes minutes, and has no deadline [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:00:17]. Garden Shop Pro lays out a fixed order for insurance money: the NAIC locator first, then missingmoney.com, then MIB only as a last resort. The channel also insists on checking every state where the person lived or worked, plus the VA, TreasuryDirect, PBGC, and HUD/FHA [HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:04:24]. The Broadstreet Radio host runs a firm that files claims for a fee, yet he still opens his long-form show by urging listeners to do the claim themselves [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:01:00]. The demutualization walkthrough on Как се прави makes the same economic point from the US side. Heir-finders charge a percentage fee, but filing directly with the state is free. Its search sequence runs Computershare and TSX Trust, then missingmoney.com, then individual state sites such as Delaware [oUFeGA0MPoM @ 00:07:27]. Baseline prerequisites also converge: a government photo ID, a signed claim form, and bank details where payment is electronic. For dead holders, add a court-issued authority such as probate, letters testamentary, a heirship order, or a letter of administration. Without those, every channel stalls at the same desk.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: For mineral money, Royalty Clerk's Texas workflow is the most granular. Search the state site (transcribed as claimitttexas.gov) by last name then first name, and add a city if results flood. Then repeat the search for relatives, maiden names, initials with and without middle names, misspellings, estate and trust names, and old family businesses. If an owner notice is in hand, search the printed property ID directly [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:02:23]. Record the reporting company on every hit, because it points to a lease that may still be producing. Blue Mesa Minerals widens the net to missingmoney.com plus the states of residence, the minerals, the operator, and Delaware. It spots royalty listings by operator names such as Mobil, Exxon, XTO, Sabine, and BP [HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:02:46]. Kansas, Texas, and Pennsylvania label entries as royalties or production payments. Texas shows exact amounts, so Blue Mesa skips claims of about 50 cents [HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:04:49]. On the paperwork, every Texas claim needs a signed form and photo ID. Proof of entitlement is a probated will, letters testamentary, or a heirship order, and an affidavit of heirship is accepted for claims under $10,000. Claims are tracked by claim ID and paid by mailed check [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:50].

Dividend recovery runs on portals and registrars. In Nigeria, the Broadstreet Radio host sends claimants to the SEC e-dividend 'unmandated' portal at sec.gov.ng, which works from abroad. Before filing, assemble a passport photograph, specimen signature, ID, bank account number, bank name, and BVN. Accepted IDs are an international passport, driver's license, or voter's card [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:04:55]. Expect an email acknowledgment the next day. Keep a small balance in the payout account for a fee he says is not 'up to 500 naira' and is rarely actually debited. One claimant got a payment alert the same day [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:05:54]. The Wealth Portfolio Builder adds the structural steps for lost certificates. First identify the registrar. Then recover the holder's CHN; you can hold many CSCS numbers but only one CHN, 'just like the BVN.' Next open a licensed brokerage account, and finally file the e-dividend mandate, which is automated at account opening [KQMVL4j21qc @ 00:03:13]. In India, GLC Wealth Advisor's guest, Advocate Ankit Girk, explains the IEPFA search by name and location, PAN, or folio. He notes the PAN route caps at about 10 searches, and says folio holders should go straight to the company or transfer agent [Rg_zkc6UGWE @ 00:05:08].

Insurance hunts run on identifiers, not names alone. Garden Shop Pro says the NAIC Locator needs name, date of birth, date of death, and SSN. It stresses the locator is 'not a search engine': the insurer contacts you, not the NAIC. After that come missingmoney.com and then MIB, which costs $75 and only covers policies after 1995 [HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:03:22]. Camille Hicks of C. Hicks Agency works the paper trail. Ask the deceased's agent, scan bank statements for premium payments, and check tax returns for cash-value interest. Then contact the insurance department of the state where the policy was purchased [_35TodkWXyM @ 00:01:46]. In India, Money9 English reports that insurers must list unclaimed amounts of ₹1,000 or more online, searchable by name, PAN, policy number, and date of birth, with data refreshed every 6 months. After 10 years the money moves to the SCWF, where it can be claimed for 25 years before going to the central government [ogkbsdCWM4g @ 00:03:20]. Holder-side numbers explain why operators now chase owners harder. PakEnergy's demo cites Texas penalties of 'almost 250k,' built from 5%, another 5% after 31 days, 10% annual interest, and $100 per day until filed. Documented owner contact resets dormancy [msbqOrpoTXc @ 00:18:08].

callout.title: Moves the Practitioners Actually Use
callout.body: Small operational moves that the practitioners report turn a one-time recovery into an ongoing payout, or stop a transfer before it happens.
items: After claiming escheated royalties, write to the operator to redirect future checks, as the heirs did in the 'Holly's Me estate' case [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:17].
Only the specific unpaid year's dividend transfers, so encashing a later year's dividend stops that year's transfer to the IEPFA [Mint — Y4d3T6BNtEg @ 00:02:24].
Get the amount due from the registrar, not the broker, before spending on recovery. 'Taking two naira to collect one naira' is unwise [Broadstreet Radio — ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:45:47].
Claiming suspended royalties can help cure title and restore pay status on the interest going forward [Blue Mesa Minerals — HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:07:55].

sop_steps.title: Run the Free Multi-Database Sweep
sop_steps.action: Search national aggregators, every state tied to the owner, and asset-specific locators.
sop_steps.detail: Search the NAIC locator, missingmoney.com, and every state of residence or work [Garden Shop Pro — HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:04:24]. For minerals, add the states of the minerals and the operator, plus Delaware [Blue Mesa Minerals — HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:00:58].

sop_steps.title: Grind Name Variants and Log Every Hit
sop_steps.action: Repeat searches across spelling variants and record the holder and request IDs for every result.
sop_steps.detail: Try relatives, maiden names, initials, misspellings, and estate and trust names, and record the reporting company on each hit [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:02:23]. Avoid stopping after one search or failing to log request IDs [Garden Shop Pro — HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:05:43].

sop_steps.title: Assemble the Entitlement Packet
sop_steps.action: Gather ID, the signed form, and estate authority before filing.
sop_steps.detail: Texas needs a signed form, a photo ID, and a probated will, letters testamentary, or a heirship order, with an affidavit of heirship accepted under $10,000 [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:50]. Indian claims need dividend warrant copies, share certificates, bank statements, self-attested Aadhaar and PAN, and a notarized death certificate and will if the holder died [Enterslice — AZAC0VeRINw @ 00:03:21].

sop_steps.title: File, Track, and Lock In Future Payments
sop_steps.action: Submit the claim, track it by ID, and redirect ongoing payments to the claimant.
sop_steps.detail: After the claim pays, write to the operator to redirect future checks [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:17]. On the Nigerian registry route, the backlog arrives first and ongoing payments follow; one client was paid 'before he could get home' [Broadstreet Radio — DLhQH9iGJ84 @ 00:04:30].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who files the claim and who gets paid for it. Broadstreet Radio's host urges listeners to run their own e-dividend claims through the SEC portal [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:01:00], yet later in the same broadcast confirms the firm will file claims for a fee [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:13:43]. Enterslice sells the outsourced version openly for Indian IEPF recoveries, promising its experts handle everything and 'only bother you for signatures' [AZAC0VeRINw @ 00:02:34]. Royalty Clerk draws the hardest boundary around Texas oil money: the finder fee is capped at 10% of what is recovered, the finder takes no share of the minerals, overriding royalty, or production payment, the agreement must be in writing, the finder cannot file the claim, and the finder must hold a DPS license [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:04:39]. The fight is really over where the margin sits. A claimant who can produce a signed form, a photo ID, and heirship proof captures the whole balance, while a paid filer earns its cut by absorbing registrar visits, notarized documents, and repeated follow-ups. Operators pitching finder work into Texas royalties must build the 10% ceiling and the license requirement into the agreement before the first owner conversation, because the cap applies to recovered dollars and never to the mineral interest itself.

Practitioners also disagree on where to start digging. Garden Shop Pro runs a fixed sequence for life benefits: the NAIC Locator first, then missingmoney.com, then MIB, whose $75 fee covers only policies after 1995 and should be treated 'as an absolute last resort' [HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:04:40]. Как се прави starts somewhere else entirely for demutualization money, going to transfer agents Computershare and TSX Trust before missingmoney.com and state sites such as Delaware, then adding the VA and NCUA [oUFeGA0MPoM @ 00:05:23]. Camille Hicks narrows the state question for lost policies to the insurance department of the state where the policy was purchased [_35TodkWXyM @ 00:02:21], while Garden Shop Pro tells searchers to hit every state of residence or work. Blue Mesa Minerals widens the net further for royalties: missingmoney.com plus the owner's states of residence, the state where the minerals sit, the operator's state, and Delaware [HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:00:58]. The common thread is that a single database never closes the file. The real disagreement is sequencing and cost, with Garden Shop Pro protecting the $75 fee, Как се прави prioritizing the agents that hold non-electors' stock, and Blue Mesa Minerals scanning listings for operator names like Mobil, Exxon, XTO, Sabine, and BP.

On the holder side, the PakEnergy and Texas Comptroller speakers expose how much the destination and the clock vary. Nikki Naylor and Joel Cox lay out the Texas v. New Jersey priority order, last-known address first, then state of incorporation, then domicile, with Oklahoma's Corporation Commission demanding forced-pool funds be sent to it instead [fVMIbCz8s0U @ 00:15:10]. The Texas Comptroller sets royalties under MI02 as abandoned after 3 years of inactivity against just 1 year for MS01 wages [rGLI7Ry3sF0 @ 00:01:45], while the PakEnergy panel flags Louisiana at 2 years, Ohio at 1, and Idaho holding 5 years, dropping to 2 when the owner is deceased. The live fight is over what counts as contact. PakEnergy reports email and ACH increasingly counting as contact, yet Idaho excludes recurring ACH as an indication of interest, and email consent remains a gray area [fVMIbCz8s0U @ 00:52:09]. PakEnergy's automation session holds that documented owner contact resets dormancy and avoids penalties [msbqOrpoTXc @ 00:45:29]. For a recovery operator, that variance decides where a listing surfaces: a New York owner's royalty lands in New York, but an address-less owner's money follows the holder's state of incorporation, so the search has to follow both trails.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures are paperwork failures on dead holders' estates. Broadstreet Radio warns that 'every letter of administration that does not mention the shares you're claiming, the instruments you're claiming is not proper,' forcing an addendum before the registrar will pay [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:11:10]. The same host puts Lagos probate at about 4 months even with well-connected lawyers, and notes the broker releases the CSCS statement only against ID showing the same surname plus a death certificate [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:11:45]. Royalty Clerk sets a hard ceiling on the shortcut route in Texas: an affidavit of heirship works only for claims under $10,000, and anything larger needs a probated will, letters testamentary, or an heirship order, on top of a signed form and photo ID [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:50]. Daggett Shuler Attorneys at Law flags the behavioral failure that kills life-insurance claims: beneficiaries 'give up too fast' when an insurer says a policy lapsed or a premium was missed, and the firm's answer is to bring in a lawyer rather than accept the denial [NbMR0Gzlwww @ 00:05:04]. Every one of these traps costs months, not dollars, so the estate documents have to name the specific shares, royalties, or policies before the claim is filed, not after a rejection letter arrives.

Search economics break down in predictable ways. Garden Shop Pro lists the mistakes that waste money: stopping after one search, paying the MIB fee early, failing to log request IDs, and falling for scammers who demand fees up front [HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:05:43]. That channel also explains why so many policies go unpaid: only about 16% of roughly 3 million annual deaths were captured in the database, with records removed from the Death Master File in 2011, and Как се прави adds that insurers skipped Death Master File checks until it led to multi-state audits [oUFeGA0MPoM @ 00:04:53]. On the small end, Blue Mesa Minerals tells royalty hunters that Texas shows exact amounts, so claims worth about 50 cents should simply be skipped [HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:04:49]. Broadstreet Radio makes the same point in naira, calling it unwise to be 'taking two naira to collect one naira,' and insisting the registrar, not the broker, is the party that confirms the amount due on a late father's shares [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:45:47]. The check every operator runs before spending is identical across continents: confirm the exact balance from the holder or registrar, then decide whether fees, probate, and travel leave anything on the table.

Holders fail too, and their failures explain why money keeps landing at the state. PakEnergy's automation session cites Texas penalties of 'almost 250k,' built from 5%, another 5% after 31 days, 10% annual interest, and $100 per day until filed [msbqOrpoTXc @ 00:18:08], with Delaware called the worst because of estimations, and sellers warned that 20-year undocumented suspense wrecks an audit trail. Nikki Naylor and Joel Cox say suspense is the most common escheatable type while AR credits are the most often missed, recalling pre-software suspense tracked across 50,000 spreadsheet lines [fVMIbCz8s0U @ 00:10:17]. Royalty Clerk spells out the owner-side cost: once a royalty escheats, later royalties keep following it to the state until the address is fixed, and late payment interest stops once the company hands the money over [8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:05:12]. Broadstreet Radio adds that unclaimed dividend money earns no interest while 'the banks are feeding fat on it' [ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:08:18]. The economics check here is time: every year a royalty or dividend sits escheated, the owner loses interest and future checks keep flowing to the state, so the claim should be paired with a letter redirecting future payments, exactly as the heirs in Royalty Clerk's estate case did.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Filing Or Pitching A Recovery
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a loss, stall, or rejection the practitioners reported firsthand.
items: Confirm the letter of administration or will names every share, royalty, or policy being claimed, or secure an addendum first [Broadstreet Radio — ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:11:10].
Size the Texas claim against the $10,000 affidavit-of-heirship ceiling before choosing between an affidavit and probate paperwork [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:50].
Log every request ID, run free searches across every state of residence or work, and refuse anyone demanding fees up front [Garden Shop Pro — HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:05:43].
Get the exact amount due from the registrar, not the broker, and walk away when collection costs exceed the balance [Broadstreet Radio — ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:45:47].

action_checklist: Search the Texas listing by last name then first name, add relatives, maiden names, initials, misspellings, estates, trusts, and old family businesses, and record the reporting company because it points to a lease that may still be producing [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:01:48].

Run missingmoney.com plus the states of residence, the minerals, the operator, and Delaware, and scan listings for operator names such as Mobil, Exxon, XTO, Sabine, and BP [Blue Mesa Minerals — HSmuF8xIaIU @ 00:00:58].

For life benefits, submit the NAIC Locator with name, date of birth, date of death, and SSN, then search missingmoney.com, and hold the $75 MIB search for last [Garden Shop Pro — HMzGGSvJ104 @ 00:03:22].
Trace hidden policies through the deceased's agent, bank statements showing premium payments, and tax returns reporting cash-value interest [C. Hicks Agency - Camille Hicks — _35TodkWXyM @ 00:01:46].
Assemble passport photo, specimen signature, ID, bank name and account number, and BVN in one file before filing on the SEC e-dividend portal [Broadstreet Radio — ykLXSnb1CRE @ 00:04:55].
After the claim pays, write to the operator to redirect future royalty checks so later payments stop flowing to the state [Royalty Clerk — 8RccEFzRtl8 @ 00:03:17].

chapters.question_prompt: How do holders manage reporting obligations, compliance exposure, and audit risks in the programs and industries covered?
chapters.title: Holder Reporting, Compliance, and Audit Risk
chapters.subtitle: Texas and Utah reporting, Tennessee negative reports, KUPS reporting technology, exposure-assessment mistakes, audit preparation and litigation, Delaware VDA invitations, enforcement penalties, and healthcare trends
chapters.executive_summary: State examiners in Utah, Tennessee, South Carolina and Texas agree with advisors at SimekScott, Friedman, Kodiak and Clarus on what triggers audits: non-filing, missing industry property types, and M&A. They also agree that receivable credit balances are where the real exposure hides. The mechanics run on hard numbers. Tennessee penalizes willful failure at $1,000 a day up to $25,000 plus 25 percent of the property value. South Carolina requires letters on items of $50 or more, sent no more than 120 days before filing. Texas sets a $250 notice floor and a July 1 deadline. Delaware gives VDA invitees 90 days before referring them to audit. Voluntary disclosure cuts the look-back to about ten years and waives penalties. The split is about posture: examiners say most holders just need training, while attorney Jennifer Borden urges holders to fight auditor overreach, even into litigation.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: State examiners and private advisors name the same three audit triggers. Clarus Partners starts with failure to file by a company with no filing history. Next come incomplete filings that leave out a property type endemic to the industry: a manufacturer that remits payables and payroll but skips receivables, an oil and gas company with no royalties, a retailer that files without gift cards [po0e86TAQwA @ 00:00:20]. The auditor in the ucproput Utah and Idaho audit-issues session describes the same flags from the state side of the table. Not reporting raises a red flag. Omitted property raises a red flag. A merger or reorg raises a red flag because records usually get lost [3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:08:16]. TNTreasury adds whistleblower complaints, randomly selected samples, and multi-state audits to the list [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:00:21]. Kodiak's Melinda Hyde draws on the firm's roughly 250 healthcare assessments and describes states mining their own databases. A holder that filed three years ago and then went quiet gets an inquiry asking whether it dissolved or was acquired. An unbroken filing history therefore works as a defense in its own right [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:19:39]. The same examiner adds a reality check on intent: most businesses simply do not know what they are doing, need training, and run smoothly once shown how. Outright fraud is very rare.

The second point of agreement is that the money that sinks companies is not in the check register. Lori, the unclaimed property principal at SimekScott, says clients treat payroll and accounts payable checks as the low-hanging fruit but miss how large accounts receivable credits can be [p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:01:18]. Managing principal Matt Bauer previously worked the state side as an auditor. Bauer says receivables drove a lot of exposure and caught controllers and CFOs off guard, because their teams chase debits and ignore customers sitting in a credit balance. The ucproput auditor puts it bluntly: companies get paid way too much, park the overpayment in receivables, and let it sit there. After three years it has to go to the state [3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:00:45]. In healthcare, Melinda Hyde of Kodiak calls active patient-account credit balances one of the largest sources of unclaimed property. No uncashed check is involved, and the state does not care whether a refund was ever processed [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:20:36]. Friedman's Alan Goldenberg and Tom Quarry warn that holders who sweep these credits into income get whipsawed. The tax is already paid, there is no statute of limitations, and there is no amended-return refund. The full amount is still owed to the state when an auditor finds it [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:15:54].

Third, every source that addresses past-due liability points the same way: disclose before you are found. Tennessee runs a Compliance Disclosure Agreement for holders not currently under audit. The holder submits a Reporting Method worksheet and its current written procedures, then comes into compliance within a set period. It avoids both the audit and the penalty fees, and the division never physically reviews its records [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:01:55]. South Carolina's Daniel Hanley describes the same lever: the treasurer's voluntary disclosure program accepts past-due property without assessing interest or penalties [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:18:20]. Friedman's Alan Goldenberg spells out the trade. An audit can reach back to the beginning of the business, while voluntary disclosure typically caps the look-back at about ten years and waives penalties. Some states also waive the due diligence requirement, provided the holder follows it going forward [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:41:49]. Clarus Partners puts the stakes in percentages: audit interest and penalty can exceed 50 percent of the liability owed in some states. It names VDAs and amnesty programs as the way to waive them [po0e86TAQwA @ 00:01:40]. Underneath all of it sits one shared prerequisite: written procedures. Tennessee requires them for entry, and Friedman notes that some states will not admit a holder to voluntary disclosure without an unclaimed property manual in place.
