sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The annual cycle follows the same five steps everywhere, but the dates and thresholds are set state by state. Utah's State Treasurer walks holders through review, due diligence, report preparation, NAUPA-format filing, and payment. Most property goes dormant at three years and payroll at one. Due diligence letters go out between May 1 and September 1, and the report and payment are both due by November 1 [hUiiEXcFE0k @ 00:01:48]. Texas runs earlier. Reports and payments are due July 1, and due diligence notices go out by mail or email 60 days before the due date, but only for property valued above $250 [WZH47JEDcEI @ 00:02:37]. South Carolina's Daniel Hanley sets the letter floor at $50 and allows letters no more than 120 days before filing. In the worked example, an October 15 filing means letters can go out no earlier than June 17. With the recommended 30-day response window, September 15 is the latest send date [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:11:40]. Friedman's Alan Goldenberg puts the general window at 60 to 120 days before the reporting date and lays out the deadlines. Most states use November 1, Maryland uses October 31, and a few use May 1. California and Puerto Rico use a two-step process in which a preliminary report comes six or seven months before the final one [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:33:41].

The filing format is fixed: states take the NAUPA electronic layout. Utah's treasurer points holders to two third-party vendors, HRS Pro and UP Exchange. Small filers can instead key in owners manually on the state portal [hUiiEXcFE0k @ 00:02:43]. Texas opens its free manual online tool to reports with 30 properties or less. It warns that property codes determine the abandonment period, so choosing the right code is the most consequential data-entry decision in the report [WZH47JEDcEI @ 00:02:57]. South Carolina refuses paper, CD, or USB and requires encrypted or password-protected electronic files. It describes UP Exchange and HRS Pro as free: sign up, download the NAUPA-formatted Excel template, build the report, and upload it [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:15:18]. At enterprise scale, Keane's pitch for KUPS is throughput. The platform runs a 14-point data validation check and two-point USPS address verification. It processes 3.5 million records and 350,000 due diligence letters per hour inside one repository that holds historical data [UP88bQoP2JU @ 00:01:30]. Deloitte runs the same job through its Intella platform. It uses proprietary workflows to calculate dormancy and exposure and lets payees respond electronically to raise response rates. Kodiak pitches a Turbo Tax model for unclaimed property and claims its exemption finds often more than cover the total cost of compliance.

The penalty schedule is the number that gets executives' attention. Tennessee charges $200 per day, up to $5,000, for negligent failure to report, deliver, or remit. Willful failure costs $1,000 per day, up to $25,000, plus 25 percent of the property value [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:02:45]. In South Carolina, penalties for a holder that simply refuses to report range from 25 percent of the property value to a $10,000 fine. However, a written extension request filed before November 1 waives late penalties and interest if the report arrives before the extension expires [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:18:36]. Delaware's VDA invitations come with a hard clock. Matt Bauer of SimekScott says a recipient must decide within the first 90 days, and declining means referral to the Department of Finance for an audit [TGu6R9Pc0-4 @ 00:00:19]. The audit math is where the real damage happens. Friedman's Tom Quarry describes contingency-fee auditors paid a percentage of what they find, look-backs of 15 to 20 years, and Delaware's estimation fraction. The auditor takes the error rate from years with records and applies it to revenue from years without them. Alan Goldenberg warns that this inflates the liability, because today's larger business gets projected onto its smaller past [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:29:42]. Kodiak adds that auto-assessed interest of 10 to 12 percent a year can push penalty and interest past the original principal.

callout.title: Moves the advisors use to shrink the bill
callout.body: Four tactics practitioners use to control audit scope, push back on auditor interpretations, and avoid over-reporting.
items: Get the list of participating states directly from each state's notification. Pam Wentz warns that the auditor's list may include every state the firm contracts with, not just the states that actually signed on [COMPUTERSHARE — 79d39hagJ6U @ 00:00:40].

Learn the statutes, regulations, and actual state practice before the auditor asks. Jennifer Borden says auditor interpretations often do not line up with what the statutes require, and holders are no longer afraid to say no, even if it leads to litigation [COMPUTERSHARE — 03CoUEgqdzg @ 00:01:47].

Hunt for exemptions before remitting. Kodiak counts about 100 healthcare exemption opportunities, including recoupment, business-to-business, and de minimis, and aims to be compliant but not overly compliant [Kodiak Solutions — 2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:28:08].

When calling a state about where to send property, give a scenario instead of a yes-or-no question. States sometimes agree to send property where the owner is most likely to look, but scale the effort to the amount: a $75 check does not justify the work a $75,000 check does [ucproput — 3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:11:13].

sop_steps.title: Map the entity footprint
sop_steps.action: Start the internal review with corporate structure, incorporation states, operating entities, and acquisition history.
sop_steps.detail: Pam Wentz calls corporate structure the single factor with the greatest effect on liability and the key to limiting an audit [COMPUTERSHARE — 79d39hagJ6U @ 00:01:28]. Melinda Hyde adds that you should pull the org chart to capture physician practices, urgent care, surgery centers, imaging, and health plans [Kodiak Solutions — 2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:23:41].

sop_steps.title: Scrub the ledgers
sop_steps.action: Review the general ledger, trial balances, voided check register, aged receivable credits, and ERP tolerance write-off settings.
sop_steps.detail: Matt Bauer flags ERPs set to write off differences within $10, which can quietly build into unclaimed credits [SimekScott LLC — p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:02:40]. Friedman reviews voided checks picked up into miscellaneous income, which typically become reportable within three to five years [Friedman LLP — duwB7Y82flc @ 00:27:10].

sop_steps.title: Run due diligence inside the window
sop_steps.action: Send owner letters inside the state's window, give owners a 30-day response deadline, and document any owner activity that stops the dormancy clock.
sop_steps.detail: South Carolina requires letters no more than 120 days before filing and recommends allowing at least 30 days for a response [SC REALTORS — D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:11:40]. A signed W-9 or a change-of-address notice counts as proof of owner awareness, while automatic drafts and interest postings do not [ucproput — 3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:06:07].

sop_steps.title: File, pay, and archive
sop_steps.action: Submit a NAUPA-format report with the correct property codes, make one payment per report, and retain the records.
sop_steps.detail: Texas requires electronic submission, payment by July 1, and retention of unclaimed property records for 10 years for later claims or audits [txcomptroller — WZH47JEDcEI @ 00:04:25].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in holder defense is whether to fold early or fight. Jennifer Borden, an attorney with Wharton Consulting Group speaking on COMPUTERSHARE, argues the era of holders acquiescing to whatever states and auditors demanded is over: with litigation now on the books, 'people aren't afraid to fight,' and if an auditor position does not feel right, Borden would say no even if that leads to litigation [03CoUEgqdzg @ 00:01:47]. The opposite playbook is the voluntary on-ramp. Friedman LLP pitches voluntary disclosure as the escape hatch: a look-back typically limited to about ten years, waived penalties, and in some states a waived due diligence requirement, versus an audit that can reach back to the beginning of the business [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:41:49]. Tennessee sells the same trade through its Compliance Disclosure Agreement, where the holder submits a proposal of Reporting Method worksheet and the division never physically reviews the company's unclaimed property records [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:02:20]. The view from the Utah audit desk undercuts the adversarial framing entirely: that auditor reports most businesses simply do not know what they are doing, want to do what's right, and run smoothly as soon as they are trained, with real fraud very rarely found [3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:07:56]. The choice is litigated finality versus a negotiated, capped exposure window.

Practitioners split on how much a holder can lean on reciprocity to shortcut multi-state filing. The ucproput Utah and Idaho presenters frame reciprocity as a holder benefit, with Utah forwarding property to all 50 states plus Puerto Rico and moving over 1 million dollars to other states in one calendar year, yet they flag the catch that a state lacking priority, Idaho included, cannot indemnify the holder for funds turned over to it [3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:04:01]. Friedman LLP is blunter: clients routinely ask to lump everything into one state report and clear the books in a single shot, and for the most part states do not allow it, with voluntary disclosure clients who try to dump everything into their state of incorporation finding it often does not work [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:35:52]. South Carolina auditor Daniel Hanley stakes out the narrow middle ground of incidental property, fewer than 10 accounts totaling less than $1,000, which most states including South Carolina will accept with an out-of-state address [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:13:46]. Kodiak Solutions shows what ignoring the split looks like: a three-hospital Indianapolis-area system reporting every vendor check and patient refund to Indiana when reports are likely due to dozens of states [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:16:36]. On this point the practitioners treat reciprocity as a small-balance convenience, not a filing strategy.

The deepest philosophical split is over how much to report at all. Kodiak Solutions vice president Jason tells healthcare holders the goal is to be 'compliant but not overly compliant,' pointing to about 100 healthcare exemption opportunities, including an exemption where a payer that never recoups its payment leaves the provider owing neither a refund nor a report, plus business-to-business and de minimis exemptions that often more than cover the total costs of compliance [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:28:08]. South Carolina's program pushes the opposite direction: all property must be reported regardless of amount, and reported accounts cannot be reduced by fees or service charges unless the act specifically allows it [D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:16:31]. Idaho sits in between as the only state exempting property valued at $50 or less, yet holders who skip reporting must keep those balances on their records indefinitely because the owner may claim at any time, so the ucproput presenter calls reporting anyway advantageous [3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:01:23]. The same tension shows up in negative reporting. Tennessee says negative reports are not required but positions a voluntary negative report, filed only through ReportItTN after due diligence turns up nothing, as one way holders can avoid an audit [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:00:45], while South Carolina generally skips negative reporting except after an approved extension.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive firsthand misses are property types holders never think to look for. SimekScott's Matt Bauer, drawing on time on the state side as an auditor, reports that accounts receivable credits drove a lot of exposure and caught controllers and CFOs off guard because receivables teams spend their time chasing debits, not customers sitting in a credit balance [p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:01:52]. Bauer adds the tolerance trap: an ERP set to write off transactions within a $10 differential, positive or negative, can quietly generate unclaimed property as credits written off outpace debits for a customer [p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:02:40]. Kodiak Solutions executive director Melinda Hyde sees the healthcare version, where one of the largest sources of property never touches accounts payable at all: active patient credit balances where no refund was ever processed, which the state treats as property the holder is holding that is not theirs [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:20:36]. The Friedman LLP presenters describe walking into major companies fifteen years ago that claimed they had none because they took it into income, then lay out the whipsaw: tax was already paid on that income, the funds still must be remitted on audit, and there is no way to amend the return for a refund [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:15:54].

Once an audit lands, the record-retention gap becomes the loss engine. Friedman LLP reports contingency-fee auditors looking for records that go back 20 years, a five-year dormancy period plus fifteen years of look-back, and when records are gone the holder falls into an estimation fraction built from known years and applied to earlier revenue [duwB7Y82flc @ 00:51:02]. Because businesses grow year over year, applying today's ratios to twenty years ago can produce a large liability that voluntary disclosure would have avoided. Kodiak Solutions confirms state audits generally reach back 15 years, far beyond most retention policies, with contingency-fee auditors incentivized to look underneath every nook and cranny [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:12:17]. Pam Wentz on COMPUTERSHARE warns these are not typical audits: they last longer, the auditors do not play by typical rules, and the participating-state list must come directly from the states, because an auditor list may include every state it has a contract with rather than the ones that signed on [79d39hagJ6U @ 00:00:40]. Jennifer Borden adds that in the last couple of years auditor interpretations have not always lined up with what statutes actually require, so holders must know the statutes, regulations, and state practice before the exam starts [03CoUEgqdzg @ 00:01:01].

The penalty math punishes delay. Tennessee sets negligent failure to report, deliver, or remit at $200 per day capped at $5,000, and willful failure at $1,000 per day up to $25,000 plus 25% of the value of the property the holder had a duty to report [KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:02:45]. Kodiak Solutions reports states increasingly auto-assess penalties plus 10% to 12% annual interest on past-due amounts, and that penalty and interest often grow larger than the original principal value of the property [2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:12:50]. M&A is the second blind spot. Clarus Partners warns that stock acquisitions, or asset transactions where liability was retained, create successor liability reaching back to the target's date of incorporation, and that these issues are generally missed in merger and acquisition due diligence [po0e86TAQwA @ 00:01:08]. SimekScott's principals add that a catch-all tax provision does not cover it; unclaimed property has to be specifically carved out in the purchase agreement, even asset deals can carry receivables with embedded property, and because VDAs and audits can take more than a year just to gather records, there is never enough time in deal diligence to size the real exposure [p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:04:30].

callout.title: Stop Points Before Exposure Compounds
callout.body: Each of these checks comes straight from a practitioner who watched holders lose money, time, or leverage by skipping it.
items: When an audit notice arrives, pull the participating-state list from the states' own notifications and never from the auditor, whose list may include every state it has a contract with [COMPUTERSHARE — 79d39hagJ6U @ 00:00:40].

Before any acquisition closes, loop in counsel with an escheatment specialty and delineate in the purchase agreement who is responsible for unclaimed property and for what periods [SimekScott LLC — p0UoXSbya5E @ 00:04:59].

Review the voided check register and stop sweeping voided or stale items into miscellaneous income, because those items become unclaimed property within three to five years [Friedman LLP — duwB7Y82flc @ 00:27:10].

If a Delaware VDA invitation arrives, decide within the first 90 days, because declining means referral to the Department of Finance for an unclaimed property audit [SimekScott LLC — TGu6R9Pc0-4 @ 00:00:19].

chapters.pull_quote: "If you fail to plan you can plan to fail... I want to know any issues before the auditors do." — Jennifer Borden, COMPUTERSHARE (03CoUEgqdzg @ 00:00:42).
action_checklist: Test your existing internal controls and make sure staff know what to review across payroll accounts, accounts receivable, accounts payable, and bank reconciliations [ucproput — 3B5mPVcKPDE @ 00:00:25].

Send due diligence letters to each owner's last known address, or by email where the owner consented, between May 1st and September 1st for Utah filings [Utah Office of State Treasurer — hUiiEXcFE0k @ 00:01:31].
Build the report in the NAUPA format using free holder software such as UP Exchange or HRS Pro, then upload directly or attach it to an email [SC REALTORS — D-PMjgNe-7s @ 00:15:18].

Pull an org chart and confirm every entity, including physician practices, urgent care, surgery centers, imaging, and health plans, plus every disbursement account, is captured in the review [Kodiak Solutions — 2BplqmdsUpU @ 00:24:01].
Run an internal review before any audit starts, beginning with corporate structure, incorporation states, and mergers or acquisitions that drive liability [COMPUTERSHARE — 79d39hagJ6U @ 00:01:12].
If past-due property exists and no audit is underway, apply for the Tennessee CDA with a proposal of Reporting Method worksheet and current written procedures [TNTreasury — KiR-ZUeCE5g @ 00:01:55].
